QS: What is the difference between .NET Framework, .NET Core and .NET 6/8/10?

.NET Framework (last version 4.8) is Windows-only and in maintenance mode; WCF and classic ASP.NET live here.|.NET Core was the cross-platform, open-source rewrite; from .NET 5 it became just '.NET', one unified platform.|Even-numbered releases (6, 8, 10) are LTS with 3 years of support; odd ones are STS. That is why we standardised on 6, then 8, and I upgraded services to .NET 10.|Benefits: cross-platform containers on Linux, better performance, built-in DI, minimal APIs, side-by-side runtimes.
Framework = Windows house, Core = portable tent, .NET 5+ = one family where even numbers stay long.

Value types (int, bool, struct, enum) hold the data itself and are copied on assignment.|Reference types (class, string, array, delegate) hold a reference to an object on the managed heap; assignment copies the reference.|Value types usually live inline (stack or inside their containing object); boxing wraps a value type into an object on the heap, which costs an allocation.|Use structs for small, immutable data; classes for identity and behaviour.
Value = photocopy, Reference = shared Google Doc link.

The compiler rewrites an async method into a state machine; at each `await` on an incomplete Task it registers a continuation and returns the thread to the pool.|No new thread is created for I/O; the thread is freed while the database, HTTP call or file read is in flight, so a server handles more requests with fewer threads.|When the I/O completes, the continuation resumes (in ASP.NET Core there is no SynchronizationContext, so `ConfigureAwait(false)` matters mostly in libraries).|Rules: async all the way, never `.Result` or `.Wait()` (deadlocks, thread starvation), avoid `async void` except event handlers, pass CancellationToken.
Waiter takes your order and serves other tables; he does not stand at the kitchen door.

A Thread is an OS-level worker; expensive to create and you manage it yourself.|A Task is a promise of future work, scheduled on the thread pool or representing pure I/O with no thread at all.|ValueTask avoids a heap allocation when the result is often available synchronously (for example a cache hit); it must be awaited only once.|In web APIs I use Task by default and ValueTask only in hot paths after measuring.
Thread = hiring a worker; Task = placing an order; ValueTask = order already on the shelf.

IEnumerable<T> iterates in memory; LINQ operators run as C# delegates on the client.|IQueryable<T> builds an expression tree that a provider (EF Core) translates to SQL, so filters run in the database.|List<T> is a materialised, in-memory collection with indexing and Count.|Classic bug: calling `.ToList()` or casting to IEnumerable too early pulls the whole table into memory before filtering.
IQueryable = send the shopping list to the shop; IEnumerable = bring the whole shop home, then pick.

An interface is a contract: what a type can do; a class can implement many. Since C# 8 interfaces may have default implementations.|An abstract class is a partial base: it can hold state, constructors and shared logic; single inheritance only.|Use an interface for capabilities and for DI/mocking (for example ISftpClient); use an abstract class when providers share real code.|In my SFTP component the common abstraction is an interface, with a base class holding shared retry and logging logic.
Interface = job description; abstract class = half-built house you finish.
Explain SOLID with examples from your work.

S: one reason to change; for example a CSV parser separate from the validator and the importer.|O: open for extension, closed for modification; adding Rebex as a new SFTP provider meant a new class, not editing callers.|L: any ISftpClient implementation (ComponentPro, SSH.NET, Rebex) can replace another without breaking the caller.|I: small interfaces; readers do not depend on write methods.|D: high-level services depend on abstractions injected through ASP.NET Core DI.
SOLID = Single job, Open door for new rooms, Liskov swap, Interface diet, Depend on plugs not wires.
Which design patterns have you used in production?

Strategy/Adapter: SFTP providers behind one interface, selected by configuration.|Factory: creating the right provider or handler at runtime.|Repository and Unit of Work over EF Core for data access in some services.|Decorator: adding retry/logging around a client without changing it.|Options pattern and Singleton (via DI) for configuration and shared clients; Observer/pub-sub through Kafka and RabbitMQ.
My code toolbox: S-F-R-D-O = Strategy, Factory, Repository, Decorator, Observer.
How does garbage collection work in .NET?

The GC is generational: new objects go to Gen 0; survivors are promoted to Gen 1, then Gen 2. Most objects die young, so Gen 0 collections are cheap and frequent.|Objects over 85 KB go to the Large Object Heap, collected with Gen 2.|The GC frees managed memory only; unmanaged resources (files, sockets, DB connections, SFTP sessions) need IDisposable and `using`.|Server GC is the default for ASP.NET Core; watch for leaks from static caches, event handlers never unsubscribed, and captured closures.
Nursery (Gen 0), school (Gen 1), retirement home (Gen 2); big furniture goes straight to the warehouse (LOH).
Delegates, Func, Action, events and lambdas?

A delegate is a type-safe function pointer.|Func<T, TResult> returns a value; Action<T> returns void; Predicate<T> returns bool.|An event is a delegate with restricted access: only the owner can raise it, others can subscribe or unsubscribe.|Lambdas are inline anonymous functions; they can capture variables (closures), which is powerful but can extend object lifetimes.
Func = function with a gift back, Action = just do it.
What is deferred execution in LINQ?

Most LINQ operators (Where, Select) do not run until you enumerate (foreach, ToList, Count, First).|Each enumeration re-runs the query, so enumerating an IQueryable twice means two database round trips.|Materialise once with ToList/ToArray when you need the results repeatedly.|Immediate operators: ToList, ToDictionary, Count, Sum, First, Any.
A LINQ query is a recipe, not a cooked meal.
How do you make code thread-safe?

Prefer immutability and avoiding shared state.|`lock` for short critical sections; `SemaphoreSlim` for async code (lock cannot contain an await) or to limit concurrency, for example parallel node deployments.|Concurrent collections (ConcurrentDictionary, Channel<T>) and `Interlocked` for counters.|Avoid double-checked locking bugs by using Lazy<T>; be careful with singletons that hold mutable state.
One key to the bathroom (lock); a bouncer counting guests (SemaphoreSlim).

class: reference type with identity; equality by reference.|record (class): reference type with value-based equality, `with` expressions and concise immutable syntax; good for DTOs and events.|struct: value type, copied on assignment; `record struct` adds value equality.|I use records for API contracts and messages published to Kafka or RabbitMQ.
Record = a receipt: two receipts with the same lines are equal.

Catch only what you can handle; let the rest bubble to global middleware that logs and returns ProblemDetails.|Use `throw;` not `throw ex;` so the stack trace is kept.|Create domain exceptions (for example StudyTransferNotAllowedException) for business rules, but do not use exceptions for normal flow.|Always log with context (correlation id, study id) and never leak stack traces to clients; use `finally` or `using` for cleanup.
Catch the ball only if you can play it; otherwise pass it to the goalkeeper (global handler).
Generics and constraints: why use them?

Generics give type-safe reusable code without boxing (List<T>, Repository<TEntity>).|Constraints (`where T : class, IEntity, new()`) let you call members safely.|Covariance (`out T`, IEnumerable<Derived> as IEnumerable<Base>) and contravariance (`in T`, Action<Base> as Action<Derived>).|Example: a generic Result<T> wrapper for API responses.
What did .NET 8/10 bring that matters for backend services?

Big runtime performance gains each release (JIT, GC, dynamic PGO) with almost free speed-ups after upgrade.|Minimal APIs maturing, native AOT for small fast-starting services, built-in rate limiting, keyed DI services (8), better OpenAPI support and System.Text.Json improvements.|Span<T>, Memory<T> and pooling for allocation-free parsing, useful in file and CSV processing.|LTS support windows drive the upgrade plan in a regulated product.
Upgrade = free horsepower plus a longer warranty.
Explain the ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline.

Each request passes through a chain of middleware components registered in Program.cs; each can act, call `next()`, or short-circuit.|The response flows back through the same chain in reverse.|Order matters: exception handling first, then HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, CORS, authentication, authorization, custom middleware (logging, correlation id), then endpoints.|Custom middleware: a class with `InvokeAsync(HttpContext, RequestDelegate next)`, or inline `app.Use`.
Airport security: each checkpoint can wave you on or stop you, and you come back through on the way out.
Explain DI lifetimes: Singleton, Scoped, Transient.

Singleton: one instance for the app lifetime (config, HttpClient factory, caches). Must be thread-safe.|Scoped: one instance per HTTP request (DbContext, unit of work).|Transient: a new instance every time it is resolved (lightweight, stateless helpers).|Captive dependency bug: never inject a Scoped service (like DbContext) into a Singleton; it lives forever and is shared across threads. Use IServiceScopeFactory instead.
Singleton = the office building, Scoped = your meeting room for one meeting, Transient = a paper cup.

Controllers: classes with attributes, filters, model binding conventions; good for large APIs with many endpoints.|Minimal APIs: lambdas mapped in Program.cs with less ceremony and slightly better performance; endpoint filters and route groups close most gaps.|Both share the same routing, DI and middleware.|I use controllers in large existing services and minimal APIs for small new microservices or tooling.
Controllers = full restaurant menu; Minimal API = food truck.
What happens at startup in Program.cs?

WebApplication.CreateBuilder sets up configuration (appsettings, environment variables, secrets), logging and the DI container.|You register services (`builder.Services.Add...`), then `Build()`.|You configure the middleware pipeline and map endpoints, then `Run()` starts Kestrel.|Kestrel is the cross-platform web server; in AWS it sits behind a load balancer.
Build the kitchen (services), lay the route (middleware), open the doors (Run).

Middleware is global, runs for every request, and knows only HttpContext.|Filters run inside MVC around actions and know action context: model state, arguments, results.|Filter order: Authorization, Resource, model binding, Action, Exception, Result.|Use middleware for cross-cutting HTTP concerns (logging, correlation id); filters for action-level concerns (validation, audit of a specific action).
Middleware = building security; filters = the receptionist on your floor.
How do model binding and validation work?

Model binding maps route, query, header and body data to parameters ([FromRoute], [FromQuery], [FromBody]).|Validation via DataAnnotations or FluentValidation; with [ApiController], invalid models return 400 ProblemDetails automatically.|Validate business rules in the service layer too, not only shape.|For CSV bulk import I validated each row and returned a per-row error report rather than failing the whole file silently.
Bind = unpack the parcel, validate = check nothing is broken.
How do you implement global exception handling?

Use `UseExceptionHandler` or an IExceptionHandler (.NET 8) / custom middleware at the top of the pipeline.|Map known exceptions to status codes (validation 400, not found 404, conflict 409) and unknown ones to 500.|Return RFC 7807 ProblemDetails with a correlation/trace id; log full detail server-side only.|This keeps controllers clean and responses consistent.
One safety net at the bottom of the circus, not one per acrobat.
REST principles, HTTP verbs and idempotency?

REST: resources identified by URIs, stateless requests, standard verbs, representations (JSON), cacheability.|GET reads (safe, idempotent); POST creates (not idempotent); PUT replaces (idempotent); PATCH partially updates; DELETE removes (idempotent).|Use proper status codes: 200, 201 with Location, 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 500.|For non-idempotent operations that clients may retry, accept an idempotency key.
Idempotent = pressing the lift button five times still calls one lift.
How do you version an API?

Options: URL segment (/api/v2/...), query string, header, or media type.|I prefer URL segment for clarity, using Asp.Versioning.|Never break existing clients: add fields, do not rename or remove; deprecate with a timeline.|Document each version in OpenAPI/Swagger.
Versioning = new edition of a book; old readers keep their copy.

Configuration layers: appsettings.json, appsettings.{Environment}.json, environment variables, user secrets, then cloud stores (AWS Parameter Store/Secrets Manager).|Bind sections to strongly typed classes with `services.Configure<T>` and inject IOptions<T>, IOptionsSnapshot<T> (per request) or IOptionsMonitor<T> (live changes).|Validate options on start (`ValidateOnStart`).|Never commit secrets.
Layers of paint: the last coat (env vars) wins.
How do you do logging and tracing in APIs?

Use ILogger<T> with structured logging (message templates, not string concatenation).|Add a correlation id middleware so one request can be traced across microservices and queues.|Ship logs to CloudWatch; build dashboards and alerts in CloudWatch and Grafana.|Log levels: Debug in dev, Information for business events, Warning/Error for problems; never log PHI or secrets, especially in a clinical system.
Every request wears a name badge (correlation id).
How do you improve the performance of an ASP.NET Core API?

Measure first: CloudWatch/Grafana metrics, profiling, slow-query logs.|Async I/O end to end; use IHttpClientFactory to avoid socket exhaustion.|Fix the database: indexes, AsNoTracking, projections, pagination, avoiding N+1.|Cache: in-memory or ElastiCache (Redis), output caching; compress responses.|Scale horizontally behind a load balancer once code is efficient.
M-A-D-C-S: Measure, Async, Database, Cache, Scale.
What is CORS and how do you configure it?

Browsers block cross-origin calls unless the server allows them via CORS headers.|A preflight OPTIONS request checks allowed origin, methods and headers.|In ASP.NET Core: AddCors with a named policy listing exact origins, then UseCors before auth.|Never combine AllowAnyOrigin with credentials.
CORS = guest list at the door, checked by the browser bouncer.
How do you make service-to-service calls resilient?

Timeouts on every call; retries with exponential backoff and jitter only for transient errors and idempotent operations.|Circuit breaker: after repeated failures, stop calling for a while (open), then test with one call (half-open).|Use Polly / Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience with IHttpClientFactory.|Add bulkheads, fallbacks and idempotency keys; for async flows prefer queues.
Circuit breaker = the fuse box at home.
REST vs SOAP (WCF) vs gRPC vs GraphQL?

REST: resource-based over HTTP/JSON; simple, cacheable, universal.|SOAP/WCF: XML envelopes, strict contracts (WSDL), WS-* security; common in older enterprise systems.|gRPC: binary Protobuf over HTTP/2, fast, streaming; good for internal service-to-service.|GraphQL: clients ask for exactly the fields they need from one endpoint; good for varied front ends.
REST = postcard, SOAP = registered letter, gRPC = phone call, GraphQL = custom order.
How do you run background work in ASP.NET Core?

Implement BackgroundService (IHostedService) for long-running loops such as queue consumers.|Create a scope inside for scoped services like DbContext.|Honour the stopping token for graceful shutdown.|For heavy or scheduled work, prefer a separate worker service, Lambda or a queue rather than doing it inside a web request.
Background service = the night shift that keeps working after the shop closes.
How does EF Core change tracking work, and when do you use AsNoTracking?

The DbContext tracks loaded entities and their state: Added, Unchanged, Modified, Deleted, Detached.|SaveChanges compares snapshots and generates INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE in one transaction.|AsNoTracking skips tracking for read-only queries: faster and less memory, ideal for GET endpoints and reports.|For bulk updates use ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete (EF Core 7+) instead of loading rows.
The DbContext is a teacher with a register: it remembers who changed.
Eager vs lazy vs explicit loading; what is the N+1 problem?

Eager: `Include` loads related data in the same query.|Lazy: related data loads on first access (proxies); convenient but causes N+1 queries.|Explicit: you call `Entry(x).Collection(...).Load()` when needed.|N+1: one query for parents plus one per child. Fix with Include, projections (`Select` into DTOs) or split queries.
N+1 = going to the shop once per egg.
How do you manage EF Core migrations in a regulated environment?

Generate migrations in code, but deploy idempotent SQL scripts (`dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent`) that are reviewed.|Apply them through the release pipeline per environment (FV, TechOps, UAT, production), not automatically at app start.|Keep migrations backward compatible so old and new app versions can run during a rollout (expand, then contract).|Version scripts with the release tag for traceability.
Expand, deploy, contract: build the new bridge before closing the old one.
How do you handle concurrency conflicts in EF Core?

Optimistic concurrency: add a rowversion/timestamp column marked as a concurrency token.|EF adds it to the WHERE clause; if no row is updated it throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException.|Resolve by reloading and retrying, merging, or returning 409 Conflict to the user.|Pessimistic locking (UPDLOCK) only for short, critical sections such as allocating limited drug supply.
Optimistic = check the version number on the ticket before you edit.

DbContext is a unit of work, registered as Scoped (one per request).|It is not thread-safe: never share it across parallel tasks.|In background services create a scope per unit of work.|AddDbContextPool reuses instances for performance in high-throughput APIs.
One DbContext per conversation; do not pass the phone around.
How do you run raw SQL or stored procedures safely in EF Core?

Use FromSql / FromSqlInterpolated or ExecuteSqlInterpolated; interpolated values become parameters.|Never build SQL by string concatenation with user input (SQL injection).|Map results to entities or keyless types.|Use raw SQL for tuned queries the LINQ provider cannot express efficiently.
How do transactions work in EF Core?

A single SaveChanges is atomic by default.|For several SaveChanges or mixed raw SQL, use `Database.BeginTransaction()` and commit/rollback.|Across services you cannot use one DB transaction; use the outbox pattern or a saga.|Keep transactions short to reduce locking and deadlocks.
All or nothing, and keep the door open for as short as possible.
What is WCF and what are its ABCs?

WCF (Windows Communication Foundation) is the .NET Framework technology for SOAP and other service communication.|A = Address (where), B = Binding (how: basicHttpBinding, wsHttpBinding, netTcpBinding), C = Contract (what: ServiceContract, OperationContract, DataContract).|It supports WS-Security, transactions and reliable messaging.|In IRT some older services expose WCF endpoints alongside newer REST APIs.
ABC: Address, Binding, Contract = where, how, what.
How would you migrate WCF services to modern .NET?

Option 1: CoreWCF, a community port that keeps SOAP contracts so existing clients do not change.|Option 2: re-expose as REST (ASP.NET Core) or gRPC and add an adapter for old clients during transition.|Move business logic into shared libraries first so the transport becomes a thin layer.|Migrate endpoint by endpoint (strangler fig), with contract tests to prove identical behaviour.
Strangler fig: grow the new tree around the old one until it can stand alone.
Walk me through how you upgraded services to .NET 10.

Situation: in [early 2026] [6] IRT services (ASP.NET Core APIs and background workers) were on .NET 8, whose support ends in November 2026. A GxP product has to stay on a supported runtime, so we planned the move to .NET 10 LTS.|Task: I owned the upgrade of [3] of those services end to end, with no change in behaviour, inside [one release cycle].|Action: I listed every project, NuGet package and Docker base image and upgraded the shared libraries first, because every service used them. Then I changed TargetFramework to net10.0, updated the SDK on the build agents, the Dockerfiles and the pipeline YAML, and updated packages such as EF Core and the test libraries. I fixed the obsolete-API and analyzer warnings listed in the breaking-change notes, and ran unit, integration and Playwright tests. On the validation environment I compared response times and memory before and after.|Result: all [3] services went through FV, TechOps, UAT and production with [no functional defects]. We measured about [10 to 15 percent] lower p95 latency and [about 10 percent] lower memory, which matches the runtime improvements Microsoft publishes.
I-T-F-T-P: Inventory, Target, Fix, Test, Promote.

Which breaking change caused you trouble?::[A shared package pinned an older Microsoft.Extensions version], which caused a version conflict. We updated it and moved to central package management (Directory.Packages.props) so versions stay aligned. Some warnings also became errors because the build uses TreatWarningsAsErrors.||How did you prove nothing changed functionally?::Full regression: unit and integration tests, Playwright end-to-end tests on the validation environment, then the FV team's formal test cycle with documented evidence before UAT and production.||What would you do differently next time?::Start the package audit earlier and keep a shared upgrade checklist, because most of the time went on third-party packages, not our own code.
Do you need Repository and Unit of Work on top of EF Core?

DbSet is already a repository and DbContext already a unit of work.|A thin repository still helps to hide query details, enforce rules (soft delete, study scoping) and make services easy to unit test.|Avoid generic repositories that leak IQueryable everywhere or just wrap every method.|My rule: add the layer when it removes duplication or protects invariants, not by default.
Do not wrap a gift that is already wrapped, unless you need a label on it.

Clustered index defines the physical order of rows; one per table, usually the primary key.|Non-clustered index is a separate B-tree with key columns and a pointer to the row; many per table.|A covering index uses INCLUDE columns so a query is answered from the index alone, avoiding key lookups.|Indexes speed reads but slow writes and use storage; index for real query patterns.
Clustered = the dictionary itself sorted A to Z; non-clustered = the index at the back of a textbook.
How did you optimize a slow SQL query?

Method: capture the query with real parameters, read the actual execution plan, fix it (index, SARGable rewrite, pagination), then measure before and after.|Situation: the site shipment list screen in IRT began timing out for a large study with [about 300] sites. It took [8 to 12 seconds] and support tickets came in.|Task: find the cause and fix it without changing what the screen shows.|Action: I got the query with real parameters from the logs and Query Store. The actual plan showed a clustered index scan on the Shipments table plus key lookups, because the filter on StudyId, Status and a date range had no matching index, and CONVERT on the date column made the predicate non-SARGable. I rewrote the date filter as a plain range (>= start and < end), added a non-clustered index on (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate) that INCLUDEs the columns the screen shows, and added server-side pagination.|Result: logical reads fell from [about 400,000 to about 2,000] and the query from [about 9 seconds to under 300 ms]. The index script was reviewed and released through FV, UAT and production like any other change.

Why that column order in the index?::Equality columns first (StudyId, Status), then the range column (ShipmentDate), so SQL Server can seek straight to the matching range. INCLUDE columns cover the SELECT, which removes the key lookups.||Did the new index slow down writes?::Slightly, but shipments are read far more often than they are written. We checked insert timings in validation and saw no noticeable change.||How do you stop it regressing?::A CloudWatch and Grafana latency alarm on that endpoint, plus the query in our performance checks before each release.

A predicate is SARGable when SQL Server can use an index seek for it.|Bad: `WHERE YEAR(CreatedOn) = 2024`, `WHERE LEFT(Code,3) = 'ABC'`, `WHERE Col + 1 = 5`, comparing NVARCHAR parameter to a VARCHAR column.|Good: `WHERE CreatedOn >= '2024-01-01' AND CreatedOn < '2025-01-01'`, `LIKE 'ABC%'`.|Rule: never wrap the indexed column in a function.
Do not put the column in handcuffs (functions), or the index cannot run.

INNER JOIN: only matching rows.|LEFT JOIN: all left rows plus matches (NULLs otherwise).|RIGHT JOIN: the mirror; FULL OUTER: all rows from both.|CROSS JOIN: every combination; SELF JOIN: table joined to itself (for example hierarchy).
Inner = handshake, Left = left side keeps everyone.

Normalization (1NF to 3NF) removes duplication and update anomalies; good for transactional systems like IRT.|Denormalization duplicates data for faster reads in reporting or NoSQL stores like DynamoDB.|1NF atomic columns, 2NF no partial dependency on a composite key, 3NF no transitive dependency.|Balance: normalized writes, denormalized read models or views.
Normalize for truth, denormalize for speed.

Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads.|Read Committed (default) prevents dirty reads; Repeatable Read also prevents non-repeatable reads; Serializable prevents phantoms too.|Snapshot / RCSI uses row versioning so readers do not block writers.|Higher isolation means more locking; choose per use case, for example serializable or locks for allocating the last kit of a drug.
Each level adds a stronger lock on the diary.
What causes deadlocks and how do you handle them?

Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs; SQL Server kills one as the victim (error 1205).|Causes: inconsistent access order, long transactions, missing indexes causing scans and wide locks.|Fix: access tables in the same order, keep transactions short, add indexes, use RCSI, retry the victim safely.|Investigate with the system_health extended event deadlock graph.
Two cars on a one-lane bridge: someone must reverse.
Stored procedures vs inline/ORM queries; what is parameter sniffing?

Stored procedures: pre-compiled plans, security via permissions, logic near data; harder to version and test.|ORM queries: easier to maintain in code, parameterised automatically.|Parameter sniffing: the plan compiled for the first parameter value is reused for very different values, which can be slow.|Fixes: OPTION (RECOMPILE), OPTIMIZE FOR, better indexes, or splitting the query.
Sniffing = the plan remembers the first customer's shoe size for everyone.
When would you choose SQL Server/RDS vs DynamoDB?

SQL Server/RDS: relational data, complex joins, strong consistency and transactions, ad-hoc reporting; the core of clinical-trial data.|DynamoDB: key-value/document, single-digit millisecond at any scale, serverless, pay-per-request; you design around access patterns (partition and sort keys).|DynamoDB is weak for ad-hoc queries and joins; SQL is harder to scale writes horizontally.|Pick by access pattern and consistency needs.
SQL = filing cabinet with cross-references; DynamoDB = super-fast lockers by key.

DELETE removes rows one by one, can have a WHERE, fires triggers, fully logged.|TRUNCATE removes all rows quickly by deallocating pages, resets identity, minimally logged.|DROP removes the table and its structure.|In regulated data, deletes are usually soft deletes with an audit trail.
Delete = erase lines, Truncate = tear out all pages, Drop = throw away the book.

OFFSET/FETCH is simple but slows down on deep pages because skipped rows are still read.|Keyset (seek) pagination uses `WHERE Id > @lastId ORDER BY Id`, constant speed and stable under inserts.|Use keyset for large lists and APIs with infinite scroll; offset for small admin grids.|Always paginate list endpoints.
Offset = counting from page 1 every time; keyset = keeping a bookmark.
CTEs and window functions; give a use case.

A CTE (`WITH x AS (...)`) names a subquery for readability or recursion (hierarchies).|Window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, SUM OVER) compute across rows without collapsing them.|Use case: remove duplicate imported rows with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY SubjectId ORDER BY ImportedOn DESC)` and keep row 1.|Also running totals of shipped kits per site.
Window function = looking at your neighbours without leaving your seat.
Unit vs integration vs end-to-end tests? What is the test pyramid?

Unit: one class in isolation with dependencies mocked; fast, many (xUnit/NUnit, Moq, Jest).|Integration: real components together, for example API plus database; fewer.|End-to-end: whole system through the UI (Playwright, Cucumber); slowest, fewest, highest confidence.|The pyramid keeps the suite fast and reliable: many at the bottom, few at the top.
Pyramid: lots of bricks (unit), some floors (integration), one roof (E2E).

xUnit: [Fact] and [Theory] with [InlineData]; a new class instance per test; setup in constructor, cleanup with IDisposable; fixtures via IClassFixture.|NUnit: [Test], [TestCase], [SetUp]/[TearDown], richer assertion model (Assert.That).|Both run in CI and report coverage to SonarQube.|I use whichever the repo already uses; consistency beats preference.
How do you use Moq, and what should you not mock?

Mock interfaces of dependencies: `mock.Setup(x => x.Get(id)).ReturnsAsync(entity)` and `mock.Verify(x => x.Save(It.IsAny<T>()), Times.Once)`.|Test behaviour and outcomes, not internal calls, wherever possible.|Do not mock what you do not own deeply (DbContext, HttpClient internals); use in-memory/Testcontainers or a fake handler instead.|Do not mock value objects or the class under test.
Mock the neighbours, not the person you are testing.
How do you integration-test an ASP.NET Core API?

Use WebApplicationFactory<Program> to host the API in memory and call it with HttpClient.|Replace external dependencies in ConfigureTestServices; use Testcontainers or a test database for SQL.|Seed data per test and clean up to keep tests independent.|Assert status codes, response bodies and side effects.
Spin up the whole shop in a box and buy something.
How do you write reliable Playwright end-to-end tests?

Use role/text/test-id locators, not brittle CSS paths.|Rely on auto-waiting and web-first assertions (`expect(locator).toBeVisible()`), never fixed sleeps.|Isolate tests with fresh contexts and seeded data; reuse auth state.|Use traces, screenshots and videos on failure to debug flaky tests in CI.
Find buttons by name like a user, not by street address (CSS path).

Behaviour is written in Gherkin: Given (context), When (action), Then (outcome).|Step definitions bind each line to code.|Business analysts and QA can read the scenarios, which helps traceability to requirements in a GxP product.|Example: Given a study with two sites, When a subject is randomized, Then a kit from the right depot is assigned.
Given-When-Then = setting, action, result: a mini story.
What is a SonarQube quality gate?

A set of pass/fail conditions on new code: coverage threshold, no new bugs or vulnerabilities, security hotspots reviewed, duplication and maintainability limits.|It runs in the CI pipeline; a failing gate blocks the merge or release.|It keeps quality from eroding, and gives auditors objective evidence.|I fix issues at source rather than suppressing them.
Quality gate = toll booth: no pass, no road.
How do you test Node.js and React code with Jest?

Jest runs unit tests with describe/it/expect, mocking via jest.fn and jest.mock.|For React, combine with React Testing Library: render, query by role, simulate user events, assert on output.|Use snapshot tests sparingly.|Run with coverage in CI.
What do you look for in a code review?

Correctness and edge cases, including null, empty, concurrency and failure paths.|Security: input validation, authorization checks, secrets, injection, safe logging (no PHI).|Design: readability, SOLID, naming, duplication, tests that cover the change.|Performance (N+1, missing async) and operability (logs, metrics). Be kind and specific; suggest, do not command.
How is testing different in a GxP regulated product?

Every requirement must trace to tests and evidence (traceability matrix).|Validation phases (FV, UAT) are formal, with documented results and sign-offs.|Changes need impact assessment and regression testing; releases follow a quality process with audit trails.|Automation (Playwright, Cucumber) speeds regression but the evidence must be stored and reviewable.
In GxP, if it is not documented, it did not happen.
How do React hooks replace lifecycle methods?

QS: ECS vs Lambda vs EC2: when do you use each?

EC2: virtual machines you manage; full control, good for legacy or special software.|ECS: run Docker containers as long-running services (on EC2 or Fargate); good for APIs and workers with steady traffic.|Lambda: functions triggered by events, pay per invocation, scale to zero; good for event handlers, glue and spiky workloads, with a 15-minute limit and cold starts.|In IRT we ran microservices on ECS behind load balancers and used Lambda for event-driven pieces.

Cluster: logical group of capacity (EC2 instances or Fargate).|Task definition: the blueprint, like a docker-compose file: image, CPU/memory, env vars, ports, IAM task role, log config.|Task: a running instance of the definition; Service: keeps N tasks running, replaces unhealthy ones, registers them with a load balancer target group, and scales.|Images come from ECR; logs go to CloudWatch.

A managed front door for APIs: routing to Lambda, ECS/HTTP backends or AWS services.|Handles authentication (JWT/Cognito authorizers, Lambda authorizers, IAM), throttling, quotas, request validation, CORS and stages.|REST APIs (feature rich) vs HTTP APIs (cheaper, faster) vs WebSocket APIs.|Logs and metrics go to CloudWatch.
API Gateway = hotel reception: checks ID, directs you, limits crowds.
What are Lambda cold starts and how do you reduce them?

A cold start happens when AWS must create a new execution environment: download code, start the runtime, run init code.|.NET can have larger cold starts; reduce with smaller packages, native AOT or ReadyToRun, SnapStart where supported, and lighter init.|Provisioned concurrency keeps environments warm for latency-critical paths.|Reuse SDK clients and connections outside the handler.
Cold start = starting a car in winter; provisioned concurrency = engine kept running.
How do you model data in DynamoDB?

Start from access patterns, not entities.|Partition key spreads data and must have high cardinality to avoid hot partitions; sort key enables range queries (begins_with, between).|GSIs and LSIs support extra access patterns; single-table design stores related items together.|Use conditional writes for optimistic concurrency, TTL for expiry, Streams to trigger Lambdas.
Partition key = which drawer, sort key = order inside the drawer.
What caching strategies do you know (ElastiCache)?

Cache-aside (lazy loading): read cache, on miss read DB and populate; most common.|Write-through: write to cache and DB together; read-heavy consistency.|Write-behind: write to cache, flush to DB later; fast but risky.|Set TTLs, invalidate on change, avoid stampedes with locking or jitter, never cache sensitive patient data without controls.
Cache-aside = check the fridge, if empty go to the shop and refill.

Application Load Balancer: layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS), path/host routing, header rules, works with ECS target groups and WAF.|Network Load Balancer: layer 4 (TCP/UDP), ultra-low latency, static IPs, millions of requests per second.|Both do health checks and spread traffic across availability zones.|For REST microservices on ECS, ALB is the usual choice.
ALB reads the letter (HTTP), NLB only reads the envelope (TCP).
What is S3 used for, and what are presigned URLs?

S3 is durable object storage: files, exports, backups, static sites, build artifacts.|Storage classes trade cost for access speed; lifecycle rules move or expire objects.|A presigned URL gives time-limited access to upload or download one object without exposing credentials.|Block public access, encrypt with SSE-KMS, and use bucket policies with least privilege.
Presigned URL = a one-time visitor pass that expires.
How do you apply IAM least privilege?

Give each service its own IAM role (ECS task role, Lambda execution role) with only the actions and resources it needs.|No long-lived access keys in code; use roles and Secrets Manager or Parameter Store.|Use conditions, resource ARNs, and review with IAM Access Analyzer.|Separate accounts or environments for dev, validation and production.
Give a key to one room, not the master key.
Describe a typical AWS network layout for microservices.

A VPC across at least two availability zones.|Public subnets hold the load balancer and NAT gateway; private subnets hold ECS tasks, Lambdas in VPC, RDS and ElastiCache.|Security groups allow only needed ports (ALB to service, service to DB).|VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB keep traffic off the internet.
Public lobby, private offices, guards (security groups) at each door.
What is infrastructure as code and why use it?

Cloud resources are defined in versioned files (CloudFormation, Terraform) instead of clicking in the console.|Benefits: repeatable environments, code review, audit trail, drift detection, easy rebuild and disaster recovery.|Very important in regulated work: every change is traceable.|Changes flow through the same CI/CD as application code.
IaC = the architect's blueprint, not hand-built each time.

CloudFormation: AWS-native, JSON/YAML templates, state managed by AWS as stacks, change sets, rollback on failure.|Terraform: multi-cloud HCL, providers for many services, explicit state file, plan/apply workflow, rich module ecosystem.|CloudFormation gets new AWS features via AWS; Terraform is better when you mix clouds or SaaS.|I have used both for ECS, Lambda, API Gateway, DynamoDB and RDS resources.
CloudFormation = AWS's own language; Terraform = translator for every cloud.
What is Terraform state and how do you manage it?

State maps resources in code to real resources and stores attributes.|Keep it remote (S3 backend with DynamoDB locking or Terraform Cloud), encrypted, never in Git.|Locking prevents two applies at once; workspaces or separate states per environment.|Use `terraform import` for existing resources and `state mv` for refactors.
State = Terraform's memory; lock it so two people do not edit at once.

Write HCL, then `terraform init` to download providers and configure the backend.|`terraform plan` shows the diff; review it in the pull request.|`terraform apply` makes the change after approval.|Run from the pipeline, not laptops; detect drift with scheduled plans.
Write, Init, Plan, Apply: measure twice, cut once.
What is drift and how do you avoid it?

Drift is when real infrastructure no longer matches code, usually from manual console changes.|Detect: CloudFormation drift detection or scheduled `terraform plan`.|Prevent: restrict console write access, all changes through pipelines, tag resources managed by IaC.|Fix: import the change into code or re-apply code.
Drift = someone moved the furniture without updating the floor plan.
Image vs container; what is a Dockerfile?

An image is an immutable, layered template; a container is a running instance of it.|A Dockerfile lists steps: base image, copy files, restore, build, set entrypoint.|Layers are cached, so order instructions from least to most frequently changing.|Containers make dev, test and production behave the same.
Image = recipe card, container = the cooked dish.
How do you write a production Dockerfile for a .NET service?

Multi-stage build: SDK image to restore and publish, small runtime (aspnet or chiseled) image to run.|Copy csproj files and restore first to cache dependencies.|Run as non-root, expose the port, add a health check endpoint, no secrets in the image.|Tag images with the build/release version and scan them for vulnerabilities.
Build in the workshop, ship only the finished product.

Pod: smallest unit, one or more containers sharing network and storage.|Deployment: desired number of pod replicas, rolling updates and rollbacks (via ReplicaSets).|Service: stable virtual IP/DNS that load-balances across pods; Ingress: HTTP routing from outside.|ConfigMap and Secret for configuration; Namespace for isolation; HPA for autoscaling.
Pod = a room, Deployment = landlord keeping N rooms ready, Service = the building's reception.
What goes in a Kubernetes Deployment YAML?

apiVersion, kind: Deployment, metadata (name, labels).|spec.replicas, spec.selector matching pod labels, and spec.template with containers: image, ports, env, resources (requests/limits).|Liveness and readiness probes; strategy (RollingUpdate with maxSurge/maxUnavailable).|A separate Service YAML selects pods by label.
Who am I (metadata), how many (replicas), what to run (template), am I healthy (probes).
Liveness vs readiness vs startup probes?

Readiness: is the pod ready for traffic? If not, it is removed from the Service endpoints.|Liveness: is it stuck? If it fails, Kubernetes restarts the container.|Startup: gives slow-starting apps time before liveness checks begin.|In ASP.NET Core expose /health/ready and /health/live with Health Checks.
Readiness = open sign on the shop; liveness = pulse check.
ConfigMap vs Secret; how do you handle configuration in containers?

ConfigMap holds non-sensitive config; Secret holds sensitive values (base64, not encrypted by default; enable encryption at rest or use an external secret store).|Inject as environment variables or mounted files.|Keep the same image across environments and change only config.|On AWS, prefer Secrets Manager or Parameter Store integrated with ECS or the cluster.
Same suitcase (image), different labels (config) per trip.
How does autoscaling work in Kubernetes and ECS?

Kubernetes HPA scales pod replicas on CPU, memory or custom metrics; Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter adds nodes.|ECS Service Auto Scaling uses target tracking (for example 60 percent CPU) or step scaling from CloudWatch alarms.|Set requests/limits properly or scaling decisions are wrong.|Scale on queue depth for consumers.
Thermostat: keep the temperature (CPU) at the target by adding heaters (pods).

Docker builds and runs containers on one host.|Kubernetes orchestrates containers across many hosts: scheduling, healing, scaling, service discovery; portable but complex.|ECS is AWS's simpler managed orchestrator, tightly integrated with IAM, ALB and CloudWatch.|We used Docker for images, Kubernetes YAML for some workloads and ECS on AWS.
Docker = a shipping container; Kubernetes/ECS = the port that moves thousands of them.
CI vs continuous delivery vs continuous deployment?

Continuous integration: every merge builds and runs tests automatically.|Continuous delivery: every build is releasable; production deploy is a manual approval.|Continuous deployment: every passing change goes to production automatically.|In a regulated GxP product we do continuous delivery with formal approval gates.
CI = always compiles, CD = always shippable, Deploy = always shipped.
Describe your Azure DevOps pipeline and release flow.

Build pipeline (YAML): restore, build, unit tests, SonarQube analysis and quality gate, publish artifacts and Docker images.|Release: deploy the same artifact through environments: FV (validation), TechOps, UAT, then production.|Each stage has approvals and checks; Ansible, Python and Shell scripts run the multi-node installs.|Release is merged and tagged so every environment is traceable to one version.
Build once, promote the same box through every gate.
YAML pipelines vs classic release pipelines in Azure DevOps?

YAML pipelines live in the repo: versioned, reviewed, templated, multi-stage.|Classic Releases are configured in the UI with visual stages and approvals; common on on-prem Azure DevOps Server.|YAML supports environments with approvals and checks; templates remove duplication.|Our MCP server talks to Azure DevOps Server APIs to trigger and monitor both builds and releases.
YAML = recipe in the cookbook; classic = recipe on a sticky note.
What branching and tagging strategy do you follow?

Feature branches off main/develop with pull requests, reviews and build validation.|Release branches cut for a version; hotfix branches from the release tag.|Tags mark exactly what was deployed (semantic version), which auditors and support rely on.|I owned merging and tagging releases across application, APIs, database and UI.
Branches are drafts, tags are the printed edition.
What role did Ansible play, and what is idempotency in it?

Ansible automates configuration and installs over SSH or WinRM with no agent, using playbooks and roles in YAML.|We used Ansible with Python and Shell scripts to install releases across multiple nodes.|Idempotent tasks can run many times and leave the same end state (for example 'ensure service is running').|Inventory files define the nodes per environment.
Ansible = a checklist robot; running it twice does not do the job twice.
Blue-green vs canary vs rolling deployments?

Rolling: replace instances gradually; no extra capacity, but mixed versions run for a while.|Blue-green: deploy to an idle copy, switch traffic at once; instant rollback, double resources.|Canary: send a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, then expand.|Choose by risk, cost and how easily you can roll back.
Rolling = change tyres one at a time; blue-green = second car ready; canary = send one bird first.
How do you plan rollback for a release that includes database changes?

Keep schema changes backward compatible (expand-contract) so the previous app version still works.|Keep the previous artifact and release tag ready to redeploy; feature flags to switch off new behaviour.|Back up before risky migrations; have tested down scripts where feasible.|Define go/no-go checks and smoke tests after deployment.
Always leave a ladder down before you climb.
How is release management different in a regulated GxP environment?

Every change links to a requirement or defect, with impact assessment, review and test evidence.|Formal environments and sign-offs: FV, TechOps, UAT, production; segregation of duties.|Validated, repeatable deployment scripts and an audit trail of who deployed what and when.|Automation helps: our MCP-driven deployments kept the steps consistent and logged, while humans kept approvals.
Regulated release = a flight checklist with signatures.
What are logs, metrics and traces?

Logs: detailed event records (what happened), structured JSON in CloudWatch Logs.|Metrics: numbers over time (latency, error rate, CPU, queue depth) for dashboards and alarms.|Traces: the path of one request across services, joined by a trace or correlation id.|Together they let you detect, locate and explain issues.
Metrics say something is wrong, traces say where, logs say why.
How do you use CloudWatch and Grafana?

CloudWatch Logs for application logs with Logs Insights queries; metrics from ECS, Lambda, ALB, RDS; alarms to notify on thresholds.|Grafana dashboards combine CloudWatch and other sources into one view for services and releases.|Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency), not just CPU.|After a release, watch dashboards for regressions.
CloudWatch collects, Grafana tells the story.

Latency: how long requests take (track p95/p99, not just average).|Traffic: requests per second or messages per second.|Errors: failure rate (5xx, exceptions, dead-lettered messages).|Saturation: how full the system is (CPU, memory, connection pool, queue depth).
How do you do root-cause analysis for a production issue?

Stabilise first: mitigate impact (rollback, scale, failover) and communicate.|Gather evidence: timeline, dashboards, logs by correlation id, recent changes.|Form and test hypotheses; use 5 Whys to go past the symptom to the real cause.|Fix, add monitoring or tests so it cannot recur, and write a blameless post-mortem.
Stop the bleeding, find the wound, prevent the next one.

Actionable: someone knows what to do when it fires; link a runbook.|Based on user impact and sustained thresholds to avoid noise.|Routed to the right owner with severity.|Reviewed regularly; delete alerts nobody acts on.
If an alert wakes you up, it must need you.

RabbitMQ: a message broker with exchanges and queues; messages are removed after acknowledgement; flexible routing; great for task queues and commands.|Kafka: a distributed, partitioned, append-only log; messages are retained and can be replayed; very high throughput; consumer groups track offsets.|Ordering: Kafka per partition; RabbitMQ per queue with one consumer.|Use RabbitMQ for work distribution, Kafka for event streams and integrations needing replay.
RabbitMQ = post office that delivers and forgets; Kafka = a diary everyone can re-read.
Explain Kafka topics, partitions and consumer groups.

A topic is split into partitions; each is an ordered log with offsets.|Producers choose a partition by key, so all events for one key (for example a study id) stay in order.|In a consumer group, each partition is read by exactly one consumer, so parallelism is limited by partition count.|Consumers commit offsets; replication across brokers gives durability.
Topic = highway, partitions = lanes, consumer group = toll booths, one per lane.

Direct: routes by exact routing key.|Topic: routes by pattern (`shipment.*.created`).|Fanout: broadcasts to all bound queues.|Headers: routes by header values. Producers publish to exchanges, never directly to queues.
Direct = named letter, Topic = postcode pattern, Fanout = flyer to every house.
What are publisher confirms and how did they fix the RabbitMQ outage?

By default a publish is fire-and-forget: if the broker is under pressure, restarts or a connection drops, messages can be lost silently.|With publisher confirms the channel is put in confirm mode and the broker acks (or nacks) each message once it is safely handled (persisted for durable queues).|The publisher tracks unconfirmed messages and retries or alerts on nack or timeout.|Combined with durable queues, persistent messages and consumer manual acks, this gives at-least-once delivery.|Situation: [one evening in mid-2024] a production RabbitMQ node hit its memory high watermark while a [large vendor shipment-status file] was being loaded. The broker blocked publishers and dropped some connections, and for [about 40 minutes] shipment-status updates from the vendor integration service never reached the shipment service. Randomization and dispensing were not affected.|Task: I was on the support rotation, so I had to restore the flow, find the root cause and stop it happening again.|Action: Grafana showed the integration service publishing normally while the incoming rate on the shipments queue had dropped to zero. The RabbitMQ management UI showed the memory alarm and blocked connections. The app logs had no errors because we published with BasicPublish and no confirms. To recover, I scaled out consumers to drain the backlog and replayed the missed window from the vendor files, which was safe because consumers upsert status by shipment id. The permanent fix was publisher confirms with tracking of unconfirmed messages, retry with backoff on nack or timeout, persistent messages on durable queues, and alerts on nacks, memory alarms and blocked connections.|Result: the replay recovered all [about 1,200] updates the same evening. In the [12 months] since there has been no silent loss, and a later broker restart produced [a few dozen] nacks that were retried automatically and showed up in alerts. The full STAR version is in part 3.
Publisher confirm = registered post with a delivery receipt.

Why did messages vanish without any error?::BasicPublish returns once the bytes are written to the socket. If the connection drops before the broker stores the message, the publisher never finds out. Without confirms there is no signal at all.||Do confirms slow publishing down?::Waiting synchronously after every message would. We track confirms asynchronously against delivery tags, which cost about [5 percent] throughput, an acceptable price for no loss.||Why not switch to Kafka?::RabbitMQ fits our command and work-queue flows. The problem was a missing delivery guarantee, not the broker, and Kafka would need the same discipline (acks=all, retries, idempotent consumers).

At-most-once: no retries; messages may be lost.|At-least-once: retries until acknowledged; duplicates possible, so consumers must be idempotent. The usual practical choice.|Exactly-once: no loss and no duplicates; only within limits (Kafka transactions) or achieved effectively through idempotency.|Design for at-least-once plus idempotent consumers.
Better to get the letter twice and ignore one than never get it.
How do you make a consumer idempotent?

Give every message a unique id; store processed ids (inbox table) and skip repeats.|Use natural idempotency: upserts, 'set status to shipped' rather than 'increment'.|Make the processed-id insert and the business update in the same transaction.|Retry with backoff, then dead-letter after N attempts.
Stamp each letter 'done' so you never act on it twice.

Messages that keep failing (or expire, or are rejected) are moved to a separate DLQ instead of blocking the main queue.|Alert on DLQ depth, inspect, fix the cause, then replay.|In RabbitMQ configure a dead-letter exchange; in Kafka publish to a retry or DLT topic.|Never silently drop clinical data messages.
What is the transactional outbox pattern?

Problem: you update the database and publish an event; if one succeeds and the other fails, systems disagree.|Solution: in the same DB transaction, write the business change and an outbox row.|A background relay reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka or RabbitMQ, marking rows sent (retry until confirmed).|Consumers stay idempotent because the relay may publish twice.
Write the letter in the same notebook as the change; a postman collects it later.

Authentication: who are you (login, token validation).|Authorization: what are you allowed to do (roles, claims, policies, resource checks like 'can this user see this study?').|In ASP.NET Core: UseAuthentication then UseAuthorization; [Authorize(Policy = ...)].|401 = not authenticated, 403 = authenticated but not allowed.
Authentication = passport check, authorization = boarding pass for a specific seat.
What is a JWT and how is it validated?

Three base64url parts: header (algorithm), payload (claims: sub, roles, exp, iss, aud), signature.|The API validates signature with the issuer's key, plus issuer, audience, expiry and not-before.|It is signed, not encrypted: never put secrets or PHI in it.|Keep access tokens short-lived; use refresh tokens to get new ones.
JWT = a sealed wristband: anyone can read it, nobody can forge it.
Explain the OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect authorization code flow with PKCE.

The app redirects the user to the identity provider with a code challenge.|User logs in (SSO); IdP redirects back with a short-lived authorization code.|The app exchanges the code plus the code verifier for tokens: access token (OAuth, for APIs) and ID token (OIDC, who the user is).|The app calls the API with the access token; the API validates it. Client credentials flow is used for service-to-service.
Code is a cloakroom ticket; only the person with the matching stub (verifier) gets the coat.
Why is logout hard with tokens, and how did you fix token-based logout?

A JWT stays valid until it expires even after the user clicks logout, because the server is stateless.|Fixes: short access-token lifetimes; revoke refresh tokens server-side on logout; a denylist of token ids (jti) checked in middleware until expiry; clear cookies; end the IdP session for SSO.|Also invalidate on password change or role change.|Situation: a [2024 security review] found that in one IRT module a JWT access token captured before logout could still call the APIs until it expired, [60 minutes] later.|Task: make logout really end access, without adding noticeable latency to every API call.|Action: I cut the access-token lifetime to [15 minutes]. On logout the server now revokes the refresh token, which is stored server-side, and writes the access token's jti to a denylist in ElastiCache (Redis) with a TTL equal to the token's remaining life. The JWT bearer OnTokenValidated event checks that denylist with one key lookup. Logout also clears the auth cookies and calls the identity provider's end-session endpoint so the SSO session ends too. I added a unit test and a Playwright test that replays an old token after logout and expects 401.|Result: the retest passed, old tokens are rejected immediately after logout, and the denylist check adds about [1 ms] per request. The fix went through review and the regulated release process.
Logout must take the wristband back, not just say goodbye.

Why not just use server-side sessions instead of JWT?::That works too, but the APIs are called by several services and scale out behind a load balancer. Keeping JWTs stateless and adding a small denylist only for logged-out tokens was the smaller, safer change.||What if Redis is unavailable?::We alert on it and fail closed for that check, returning 401 so the user logs in again, because accepting a revoked token is worse than an extra login. The short token lifetime limits exposure either way.||Why a TTL on denylist entries?::Once the token's own expiry passes, it is rejected anyway, so the entry can expire. That keeps the denylist small.
What causes 'request header too long' with SSO cookies, and how did you fix it?

Servers limit total request header size (IIS, Kestrel, load balancers, often 8 to 16 KB).|SSO tokens with many claims or groups, stored in cookies, can exceed it; chunked auth cookies add up across apps on the same domain.|Fixes: trim claims, store the session server-side and keep only a reference in the cookie, scope cookie domain and path, clean stale cookies; raising limits is a last resort.|Situation: in [2024] some users, mostly [study managers with access to many studies], got 'HTTP 400: the size of the request headers is too long' straight after SSO login, while other users were fine. We had [about 30] support tickets over [two weeks].|Task: find out why only some users failed and fix it permanently.|Action: I reproduced it with a test user given many role and study groups. ASP.NET Core cookie authentication was storing every role and group claim in the auth cookie and splitting it into [5] chunks of about [13 KB] in total. Together with other apps' cookies on the same parent domain, the Cookie header passed the [16 KB] request-header limit of the IIS/http.sys front end. I removed group and role claims from the cookie by storing the authentication ticket server-side through an ITicketStore, so the cookie holds only a session key, and loaded study-level permissions per request through claims transformation with caching. I also narrowed the cookie path and domain so sibling apps' cookies were not sent, and cleared old cookie names.|Result: the auth cookie fell from [about 13 KB to under 1 KB], affected users could log in again, and I added a regression test with a user in [200+] groups. We did not raise the server limits.
Do not carry your whole wardrobe in your pocket; carry the locker key.

Why not just increase the header size limit?::It only moves the problem. The next user with more groups fails again, and every request carries a big cookie, which wastes bandwidth and exposes more data. Shrinking the cookie fixes the cause.||What is an ITicketStore?::An ASP.NET Core cookie-auth extension point that stores the authentication ticket server-side (for example in Redis or SQL) and puts only a key in the cookie.||Did loading permissions per request slow things down?::They are cached per user for a short time, so the cost was negligible, and permission changes take effect faster than with claims baked into a cookie.

Tell me about the RabbitMQ outage you root-caused.

Situation: [one evening in mid-2024] a production RabbitMQ node hit its memory high watermark while a [large vendor shipment-status file] was loading. The broker blocked publishers and dropped some connections. For [about 40 minutes] shipment-status updates from the vendor integration service never reached the shipment service, so [some sites saw stale shipment statuses]. Randomization and dispensing were not affected.|Task: I was on the support rotation, so I had to restore the flow, find the root cause and prevent a repeat.|Action: a CloudWatch alarm on consumer inactivity fired. Grafana showed the integration service publishing normally while the incoming rate on the shipments queue had dropped to zero. The RabbitMQ management UI showed the memory alarm and blocked connections. The app logs had no errors because we published with BasicPublish and no confirms, so messages lost during connection resets were invisible. I scaled out consumers to drain the backlog and replayed the missed window by re-processing the vendor files, which was safe because consumers upsert status by shipment id. The permanent fix: publisher confirms with tracking of unconfirmed messages, retry with backoff on nack or timeout, persistent messages on durable queues, consumers that ack only after committing, and alerts on nacks, memory alarms and blocked connections. I wrote the post-mortem.|Result: the replay recovered all [about 1,200] updates the same evening. In the [12 months] since there has been no silent message loss, and a later broker restart produced [a few dozen] nacks that were retried automatically and showed up in alerts.

Why did the broker block publishers?::When RabbitMQ crosses its memory high watermark it raises a memory alarm and blocks publishing connections until memory falls, to protect itself. Slow consumers plus a burst of messages caused it.||Did confirms slow publishing?::We track confirms asynchronously instead of waiting after each message, so throughput dropped only about [5 percent].||How did you know the replay would not create duplicates?::Consumers upsert by shipment id and ignore a status older than the one stored, so processing a message twice leaves the same result.
