An API is suddenly slow in production. What do you do?

Check dashboards: is it all endpoints or one, since when, did a release or traffic spike happen?|Look at latency by dependency: database, downstream services, CPU/memory, thread pool, connection pool.|Use logs and traces with correlation ids to find the slow step; check slow queries and execution plans.|Mitigate (scale out, rollback, cache), then fix the root cause and add an alert.|Situation: one morning in [March 2025] the shipments API's p95 latency jumped from [about 200 ms to about 3 seconds] during the European peak, with no release that day.|Task: I picked up the alert and had to restore normal latency.|Action: Grafana showed database latency up and CPU normal. CloudWatch logs, filtered by correlation id, pointed to one query. Query Store showed its plan had changed after an overnight statistics update, a parameter-sniffing case where a plan compiled for a tiny study was reused for large ones. I forced the previous good plan in Query Store within [about 20 minutes], then rewrote the query and added a covering index so any plan performs well.|Result: latency returned to [about 200 ms] and has not recurred, and I added a p95 alarm on that endpoint.

What is plan forcing in Query Store?::Query Store keeps the history of plans per query. You can force a known good plan so the optimizer uses it, which is a fast, reversible mitigation.||Why not just restart the service?::The problem was in the database plan, not the app, so a restart would not have helped. Evidence first, then action.
Memory keeps growing in a .NET service until it restarts. How do you investigate?

Confirm with metrics that memory grows steadily, not just GC behaviour.|Take memory dumps (dotnet-dump, dotnet-gcdump) at two points and compare the biggest growing object types.|Common causes: static caches without limits, event handlers not unsubscribed, undisposed HttpClient/streams, singletons holding scoped objects.|Fix, load test, and add memory alarms.|Situation: an ECS worker service's memory grew by [about 150 MB a day], and tasks were killed for running out of memory every [about 3 days].|Task: find the leak and stop the restarts.|Action: I took dotnet-gcdump snapshots a few hours apart and compared them. The growth was in a static ConcurrentDictionary that cached study configuration per study and version with no eviction. I replaced it with IMemoryCache with a size limit and a [30-minute] sliding expiration, then ran an overnight load test.|Result: memory stays flat at [about 350 MB], and I added a CloudWatch alarm at [80 percent] of the task's memory.
Two snapshots, compare, find the hoarder.

gcdump vs a full memory dump?::A gcdump captures only the managed heap graph, so it is small and safe to take in production. A full dump has everything (including possibly sensitive data) and is much bigger.||Why do static caches leak?::A static field lives for the whole process, so anything added and never removed stays in memory forever.
After a release, 500 errors spike. What do you do?

Decide fast: if impact is high, roll back to the previous tagged release.|Look at error logs for the new exception and the endpoints affected.|Check what changed: code, config, database migration, infrastructure.|Fix forward with tests or re-release; write up the cause and add a test or check to the pipeline.|Situation: after a release to [UAT], 5xx errors on one API rose to [about 8 percent].|Task: as release owner, restore the environment and fix the cause.|Action: the logs showed a configuration-binding exception because a new required setting existed in appsettings but not in the UAT environment's parameters. I rolled back within [15 minutes], added the setting, and changed the options to use ValidateOnStart, so a missing setting now fails at startup (the health check fails and the deployment stops) instead of on live requests. I also added a configuration item to the release checklist.|Result: the next-day re-release was clean, and this class of error now stops the deployment instead of reaching users.

Why roll back before fixing?::Rollback is fast and known to work. Investigating while users or testers are blocked costs more than a redeploy later.||Why does ValidateOnStart help?::It validates configuration when the app starts, so a broken config makes the deployment fail visibly instead of producing 500s later.
Messages seem to be missing between two services. How do you debug it?

Trace one message by id: was it published, did the broker accept it, is it in a queue, DLQ, or was it consumed?|Check publisher confirms, queue depths, consumer errors and acks.|Check for consumers acking before processing, or exceptions swallowed.|Fix the gap and add monitoring on queue depth and DLQ.|Situation: in [validation] testers reported that [a few] kit-assignment notification messages went missing now and then.|Task: find where they were lost.|Action: I traced message ids. They were published, confirmed by the broker and delivered, but the consumer used autoAck=true, so when processing threw a transient database timeout the message was already gone. I switched to manual ack after the database commit, added a retry policy of [3] attempts with backoff, then a dead-letter queue with an alert.|Result: no more missing messages, and [two] messages that later reached the DLQ were replayed after the cause was fixed.
Follow the parcel: sent, sorted, delivered, signed.

autoAck vs manual ack?::With autoAck the broker deletes the message as soon as it is delivered. With manual ack it waits until the consumer confirms success, so a crash or exception means redelivery.||What is a poison message and how do you handle it?::A message that always fails. Limit retries, then move it to the DLQ so it does not block the queue, and alert someone.
A multi-node deployment fails on one node only. What do you do?

Stop the rollout so nodes do not drift further apart.|Compare the failing node: logs from Ansible/scripts, disk space, permissions, service state, config, versions.|Fix and rerun the idempotent step on that node, then verify all nodes are on the same version.|Add a pre-check for that condition to the automation or MCP tool.|Situation: a UAT deployment failed on node [3 of 5] because the service would not start.|Task: finish the deployment and stop it happening again.|Action: I paused the rollout. The Ansible output showed the files copied but the service failed to start, and the node's event log showed the disk was [98 percent] full from old release folders and unrotated logs. I removed old releases (keeping the last [2]), re-ran the idempotent step on that node, and confirmed all nodes reported the same version. I then added a prerequisite-check tool to the CIRT MCP server (disk space, service state) and a cleanup step in the scripts.|Result: the deployment finished [about 45 minutes] later, and it has not recurred.
Odd one out: compare it to its healthy siblings.

Why pause the rollout?::To avoid nodes running different versions, which is harder to support and to validate.||Why can you safely re-run the step?::The install steps are idempotent: they check the current state and only change what differs.
Database deadlocks suddenly increase. How do you respond?

Capture deadlock graphs from system_health extended events.|Identify the queries and resources involved; often a new query or missing index causing scans.|Fix access order, shorten transactions, add the index, consider RCSI.|Add safe retry for deadlock victims.|Situation: after a release, deadlock errors (1205) appeared [about 20 times a day] on inventory updates during kit assignment.|Task: find the cause and remove it.|Action: the system_health deadlock graph showed kit assignment updating Inventory then Shipment, while the resupply job updated Shipment then Inventory, the opposite order. A missing index on Inventory (SiteId, Status) also caused scans and wider locks. I changed the resupply job to the same table order, added the index, shortened the transactions, and added retry for error 1205 (EF Core EnableRetryOnFailure).|Result: deadlocks fell to [about one a week or fewer], and the occasional victim is retried automatically.
Read the graph, untangle the lanes.

Why does access order matter?::If every transaction locks tables in the same order, no cycle of waiting can form, so no deadlock.||Is retry alone enough?::No. Retry hides symptoms; fixing the order and the index removes the cause, and retry handles the rare leftover.
A vendor says they did not receive a file over SFTP. How do you handle it?

Check our job logs: did the upload run, which provider, any errors or retries?|Verify on the server: file present, size, name, path, permissions; check host key or credential changes.|Re-send if safe (idempotent naming) and confirm with the vendor.|Add alerts for failed transfers and a confirmation step if missing.|Situation: [one Monday] a depot vendor said our daily order file had not arrived.|Task: get the orders to them quickly and find out why.|Action: our job logs showed a successful upload to the /outbound folder, but over the weekend the vendor had moved their pickup folder to [/inbound/irt], announced in an email to a different team. I confirmed the file was in the old folder, re-sent it to the new path with the same file name (the vendor de-duplicates by name), and confirmed with them. I then added a post-upload check that lists the remote folder, alerts on failed transfers, and a change process for vendor connection settings.|Result: the vendor processed the orders [the same morning], with no shipment delay.
Did it leave, did it arrive, can they see it?

How do you make a re-send safe?::Deterministic file names and vendor-side de-duplication, so sending the same file twice cannot create duplicate orders.||How do you prevent it next time?::Vendor connection details are changed only through a tracked change, with a test transfer before go-live.
A Kubernetes pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. What do you check?

`kubectl describe pod` for events: image pull errors, OOMKilled, failed probes.|`kubectl logs --previous` for the app's startup exception.|Check config and secrets, resource limits, and whether liveness probes kill a slow-starting app.|Fix and redeploy; add a startup probe if needed.|Situation: a new version of a Node.js tooling service went into CrashLoopBackOff in the [dev] Kubernetes cluster.|Task: get it healthy and fix the deployment template.|Action: kubectl describe showed liveness probe failures. kubectl logs --previous showed the app needed [about 40 seconds] to warm up (loading configuration and a cache), while the liveness probe started after [10 seconds] and killed it. I added a startupProbe allowing [60 seconds] and made part of the warm-up lazy.|Result: the pods became healthy, and I updated the service template so other services get a startup probe by default.

Why a startup probe instead of a longer liveness delay?::A startup probe protects only the start. Liveness can then stay strict, so a hung container is still restarted quickly later.||Liveness vs readiness?::Readiness failure removes the pod from traffic; liveness failure restarts it.
A Lambda function is timing out. How do you fix it?

Check CloudWatch logs and duration metrics: always or only on cold start?|Find the slow call: VPC networking/NAT, database connections, downstream APIs.|Increase memory (more CPU too), reuse connections, add timeouts, or move long work to a queue or ECS.|Set alarms on errors and duration.|Situation: a Lambda processing DynamoDB stream events for [shipment notifications] started timing out at [30 seconds] as volume grew.|Task: stop the timeouts without losing events.|Action: CloudWatch showed timeouts mostly on large batches, and the logs showed an HTTP client created on every invocation and a slow downstream API called with no timeout. I moved the client outside the handler, set a [5-second] HTTP timeout with retry, reduced the batch size from [100 to 25], enabled ReportBatchItemFailures so only failed records are retried, and raised memory from [512 MB to 1 GB].|Result: p99 duration is about [4 seconds], with no timeouts since.
Where is it waiting? Give it muscle or split the job.

What does ReportBatchItemFailures do?::The function returns the ids of failed records, and Lambda retries only those instead of the whole batch, which avoids reprocessing and endless loops.||Why does more memory help?::Lambda gives CPU in proportion to memory, so more memory also means faster code and TLS setup.
Users report they are logged out randomly or SSO fails for some users. How do you approach it?

Find the pattern: which users, browsers, apps, times; check whether those users have many groups or claims.|Inspect the request: cookie and header sizes, token expiry, clock skew, cookie domain/path conflicts.|Check server and load balancer header limits and auth logs.|This is how 'header too long' issues show up; fix the cause (smaller cookies, server-side session) rather than only raising limits.|Situation: in [2024] we had [about 30] tickets over [two weeks], mostly from study managers with many study groups, about 400 errors right after SSO login.|Task: find the pattern and fix the cause.|Action: I reproduced it with a test user in many groups. The chunked auth cookie held every claim, about [13 KB], and with other cookies the header passed the [16 KB] IIS/http.sys limit. I moved the auth ticket to a server-side ITicketStore and loaded permissions per request with caching.|Result: the cookie shrank to [under 1 KB], the tickets stopped, and a regression test now covers a user in [200+] groups.
Pattern first: who fails tells you why.

How did you reproduce it?::Created a test user, added them to many groups until the failure appeared, and measured the Cookie header in browser dev tools.||Why did only some users fail?::Cookie size grows with the number of groups and claims, so only users above a certain number of groups crossed the limit.
Your SonarQube quality gate fails just before a release. What do you do?

Look at what failed: new bugs, vulnerabilities, coverage on new code, duplication.|Fix real issues; add missing tests; never mark true issues as false positives to pass.|If it is a genuine false positive, document and get it reviewed.|Talk to the release owner early if it threatens the date.|Situation: [two days] before code freeze, the gate failed: coverage on new code was [68 percent] against an [80 percent] threshold, and SonarQube flagged a hard-coded test connection string as a vulnerability.|Task: get the gate green honestly without slipping the release.|Action: I moved the connection string to user secrets and a pipeline variable, spent [about half a day] writing the missing tests for new validator branches, and updated the release owner that morning.|Result: the gate was green the next day with no date slip and no suppressed issues.
Fix the code, not the gate.

Is a coverage target meaningful?::It is a floor, not a goal. Meaningful tests on new logic matter more than the number, but the gate stops untested code slipping in.||What about false positives?::Mark them only with a written reason and a reviewer's agreement, never just to pass.
A unit test passes locally but fails in CI. How do you debug?

Look for environment differences: time zone, culture, file paths, OS (Linux agents), env variables.|Check test order dependence and shared static state; xUnit runs test classes in parallel.|Check timing assumptions and async code without awaits.|Reproduce with the same container or agent image.|Situation: a date-formatting unit test passed on my Windows laptop but failed on the Linux build agent.|Task: make it reliable everywhere.|Action: the test expected a dd/MM/yyyy string, but the agent ran with a different culture (en-US). The code used the current culture implicitly. I changed it to format with an explicit culture where a fixed format is required, and made the test set its culture explicitly. I reproduced and verified it in the same .NET SDK container image the agent uses.|Result: the test is stable, and I now run tests in the SDK container before pushing changes that depend on culture or time zone.
It is not magic; it is a difference. Find the difference.

How do you prevent this class of bug?::Pass CultureInfo explicitly for parsing and formatting, inject time through TimeProvider, and run tests in the same container as CI.||What else commonly differs between local and CI?::File path separators and case sensitivity on Linux, environment variables, parallel test execution and time zones.
An AI agent suggested a code change that looks right but you are not sure. What do you do?

Read it critically and check APIs against official docs.|Build it, run tests, add a test for the new behaviour.|Run SonarQube and security checks; look for hallucinated packages or methods.|If still unsure, ask a colleague to review; never merge code you cannot explain.|Situation: Copilot suggested a retry policy for our Azure DevOps API client that retried every failure, including the POST that creates a release.|Task: decide whether to accept it.|Action: I noticed that retrying a non-idempotent POST after a timeout could create duplicate releases. I checked the API docs, limited retries to GET calls and transient status codes (408, 429, 5xx) with exponential backoff, and added a unit test proving that a POST is not retried.|Result: the client is resilient without risking duplicate releases, and I shared the example with the team as a reminder to review AI output.
If I cannot explain it, I do not ship it.

What else do you check in AI-generated code?::Hallucinated APIs or packages, missing authorization checks, swallowed exceptions, sync-over-async, and secrets or PHI in logs.||Do you tell the team about such catches?::Yes, short examples in team chat help everyone review AI output better.

Situation: one or two lines of context.|Task: what you were responsible for.|Action: what you did, in first person, with technical detail (this is the longest part).|Result: the outcome with real numbers where you have them, plus what you learned.

Situation: [mid-2024], a production RabbitMQ node hit its memory alarm, and for [about 40 minutes] shipment-status updates silently stopped reaching the shipment service.|Task: as the person on support, restore the flow and find the cause.|Action: I used CloudWatch and Grafana to see that publishing looked normal while the queue received nothing, found the memory alarm and blocked connections in RabbitMQ, and realised publishes had no confirms. I added unit tests for several time zones using a fake clock (TimeProvider), and added a time-zone item to my pull-request checklist.|Result: fixed within [a day], caught in FV rather than production, and I have not shipped a time-zone bug since.
Own it, fix it, prevent it.

The real failure would have been reaching production, and the fix made sure the same class of bug is now tested automatically.

C# with ASP.NET Core Web API, EF Core and SQL Server: I have used them daily for 4+ years on IRT, including the .NET 10 upgrade.|Close behind: messaging (RabbitMQ, Kafka), AWS deployment, CI/CD and release automation, and AI-assisted engineering through MCP.

C#/.NET, ASP.NET Core, EF Core and SQL Server for features; Git and Azure DevOps for pull requests and pipelines.|CloudWatch and Grafana for monitoring, RabbitMQ and Kafka for events, xUnit, Moq and Playwright for tests.|GitHub Copilot and Cursor, with the CIRT MCP server for deployments.
What was the most challenging project you worked on?

Situation: the CIRT MCP server. Deployments on on-prem Azure DevOps Server were multi-node and took about 6 hours and about 6 people.|Task: automate them safely in a regulated product, on my own, without disturbing live releases.|Action: I mapped [about 30] manual steps, built read-only tools first, then write tools with confirmations, polling for long-running jobs and per-user credentials, growing to about 77 tools.|Result: 6 hours to 2 and 6 people to 1. The hard part was safety and tool design, not code volume.

Why was safety the hard part?::An agent can call any tool it sees, so every write tool needed input validation, allow-lists, confirmation before risky steps and audit logging, while keeping the existing human approvals.||What would you do differently?::Write the tool-naming and description guidelines first; I refactored names [twice] when the model picked the wrong tool.
Tell me about a technical decision you made.

Situation: for the CSV bulk import we had to choose between partial imports and all-or-nothing saves.|Task: I owned the design.|Action: I compared audit and rollback risk in GxP with user experience, proposed a validate-only preview followed by an all-or-nothing transactional save, and agreed it with the BA and QA lead.|Result: live in production with no half-imported studies, and users see every error before saving.
Preview first, then all or nothing.

What alternatives did you reject?::Partial import (risky half-configured studies) and a staging table that users edit (more UI and audit work for little gain).||How did you validate the decision?::FV testing with large and broken files, and no support tickets about partial data since release.
Tell me about a time you improved an existing system.

Situation: vendor file transfers were tied to one SFTP library (ComponentPro), and in [2024] [a depot vendor hardened their server], which broke our connection.|Task: make the integration robust so a library change would not touch business code.|Action: I put all providers behind a common ISftpClient with a factory and a base class for shared retry and logging, added Rebex, and switched vendors one at a time by configuration.|Result: Rebex is in production with [no failed transfers caused by the switch], and future library changes are one class plus configuration.
Swap the plug, not the wiring.

How did you avoid breaking existing transfers?::Same interface, integration tests against a test SFTP server, and a gradual rollout starting with [one low-volume vendor] with the old provider as a fallback.
What kind of role are you looking for?

A senior backend or API engineer role on .NET, with AWS and event-driven systems, owning the design and delivery of services.|Room to keep using AI-assisted engineering and build developer tooling, and to mentor others.|A product with real scale and quality standards.
What are you expecting from your next organization?

Bigger ownership of design decisions and production systems.|A strong engineering culture: code reviews, CI/CD, observability and time to learn.|A modern stack, openness to AI tools, and a clear growth path to senior or lead.

My first job at DXC was C#/.NET, and I stayed because it suits enterprise backends: strong typing, excellent tooling, high performance, first-class async and DI, and cross-platform containers since .NET Core.|Microsoft's LTS release cadence also fits a regulated product.
Why did you move toward AI?

I did not move away from backend; AI multiplies it. I saw deployments eating 6 people and 6 hours, and MCP let agents run those steps safely.|I use AI where it removes toil (deployments, tests, log triage) and keep humans on approvals and design.
AI is a power tool for backend work.
Why do you consider yourself full-stack?

I build backend services and APIs, and also React/TypeScript components and Angular modules in the IRT UI, plus Playwright tests and the deployment pipeline.|So I can take a feature from database to screen to production, while my depth stays in the backend.
Which technology are you strongest in?
C#/.NET backend: ASP.NET Core, EF Core, SQL Server, plus distributed-system basics such as messaging and resilience.|Close second: CI/CD and release automation.
Which technology are you weakest in?

Java/Spring Boot: I have worked on services but I am much stronger in .NET. I can read, fix and extend Spring code and would ramp up quickly because the concepts map one to one.|Also Kubernetes cluster administration: I deploy to it, but platform teams run the clusters.
Which technology would you choose for a new project?

It depends on the team and workload. For a core domain service: ASP.NET Core on .NET 10 LTS, EF Core with SQL Server or DynamoDB, containers on ECS, Terraform, and RabbitMQ or Kafka for events.|Node/TypeScript for I/O glue and tooling, Python for data and AI scripting.
If we remove AI from your profile, what is your core strength?

Shipping reliable .NET backend services in a regulated environment: APIs, data, messaging, production troubleshooting (the RabbitMQ outage, SQL and SSO fixes) and release ownership across FV, TechOps, UAT and production.|The MCP server itself is backend engineering: APIs, orchestration and security.
Without AI: a reliable backend engineer who owns production.
How much of your resume work was individual vs team-based?

Individual: the CIRT MCP server (solely authored), SFTP component ownership, the Rebex release, the study-transfer guard and several production RCAs.|Team: IRT microservices, the .NET upgrade (I owned [3 of 6] services), the CSV import (I owned the design and most of the build) and releases across [5] scrum teams.|I say I for my parts and we for team work.
Say I for mine, we for ours.
What are the main OOP principles?
Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.|Together they hide details, model contracts, reuse code and swap behaviour at runtime, for example ISftpClient with three providers.
A PIE: Abstraction, Polymorphism, Inheritance, Encapsulation.

Bundle data with the methods that change it and hide internal state behind a public surface (private fields, properties, methods that enforce rules).|Example: a Shipment exposes `MarkDelivered()` that validates the status, instead of a public settable Status.
Capsule: only the pill's surface is visible.

A class derives from a base class to reuse and extend its behaviour (an is-a relationship).|Example: SftpClientBase holds retry and logging; each provider class inherits it.|Prefer composition when the relationship is has-a or behaviour varies a lot.
The child gets the parent's toolbox.

One interface, many implementations: the method that runs is chosen at runtime (virtual/override, interfaces) or at compile time (overloading).|Example: code calls `ISftpClient.UploadAsync`, and Rebex or SSH.NET runs depending on configuration.
Expose what something does and hide how it does it; interfaces and abstract classes model the essential contract.|Callers depend on ISftpClient without knowing any library details.
A class is the blueprint (the type definition); an object is an instance created from it at runtime, with its own state.

Overloading: same method name with different parameters in the same class, resolved at compile time.|Overriding: a derived class replaces a virtual base method with the same signature, resolved at runtime.
`virtual` in the base class marks a method as replaceable; `override` in the derived class supplies the new implementation.|A call through a base-class reference runs the override (runtime dispatch).
Virtual = may be replaced; override = replaced.
new vs override, and what is method hiding?

`override` replaces a virtual method, so base-typed references call the derived version.|`new` hides the base method (method hiding): which one runs depends on the reference's declared type, a common source of bugs.|Use override for polymorphism; use new only for deliberate shadowing.
Override = real replacement; new = a disguise.
What is a sealed class, and a sealed method?
A sealed class cannot be inherited (string is sealed); a sealed override stops further overriding down the chain.|Use it for design intent and safety; it also lets the JIT devirtualize calls.
Sealed = end of the family line.

Stack: per-thread LIFO memory for method frames, locals and value types; very fast and freed when the method returns.|Heap: shared managed memory for objects (reference types), cleaned by the GC.|A value type lives where it is declared: as a field of an object it is on the heap.
Stack = sticky notes on your desk; heap = warehouse with a cleaner.
Boxing wraps a value type in an object on the heap (int to object); unboxing casts it back.|It costs an allocation and GC work; avoid it with generics (List<int>, not ArrayList).
Boxing = putting a coin in a gift box.
What is IDisposable, the using statement and the using declaration?

IDisposable.Dispose releases unmanaged resources (connections, streams, SFTP sessions) deterministically.|`using (var x = ...) { }` calls Dispose at the end of the block, even on exceptions; the C# 8 using declaration `using var x = ...;` disposes at the end of the scope.|For async cleanup: IAsyncDisposable with `await using`.
const vs readonly vs static readonly?

const: compile-time constant, implicitly static, baked into calling assemblies.|readonly: set at declaration or in the constructor, per instance.|static readonly: set once per type at runtime (good for objects like a TimeSpan or a Regex).
const = carved in stone; readonly = set at birth.
What are ref, out and in?
ref: pass by reference; must be initialised; the callee may change it.|out: the callee must assign it; used for TryParse-style methods.|in: read-only reference that avoids copying large structs.
ref = two-way, out = return slot, in = look but don't touch.

A C# 8 feature: reference types are non-nullable by default and `string?` marks a nullable one; the compiler warns on possible null dereferences.|It catches NullReferenceException bugs at compile time; we enable it in new projects.

Concise testing and deconstruction of values: type patterns with `is`, switch expressions, property patterns, relational and list patterns.|Example: `var fee = s switch { { Express: true } => 20, { Weight: > 10 } => 12, _ => 5 };`

Static methods in a static class whose first parameter is `this T`, callable as if they were instance methods.|LINQ is built on them; we use them for DI registration such as `services.AddSftpProviders()`.
Bolt-on methods without touching the class.

A named set of integer constants, such as `enum ShipmentStatus { Created, Shipped, Delivered }`; type-safe and readable.|[Flags] enums combine values bitwise; decide deliberately whether to store them as int or string in the database.
What is deadlock in async code?

Blocking on async code (`.Result`, `.Wait()`) when a SynchronizationContext (WinForms, classic ASP.NET) needs the blocked thread to run the continuation: each waits for the other forever.|ASP.NET Core has no such context, so it shows up as thread-pool starvation instead.|Fix: async all the way, and ConfigureAwait(false) in libraries.
Holding the door while waiting for someone who needs that door.

`ConfigureAwait(false)` tells await not to resume on the captured SynchronizationContext.|Useful in libraries and UI apps to avoid deadlocks and context switches; mostly unnecessary in ASP.NET Core app code.

Language Integrated Query: one syntax to query collections, databases (EF Core) and XML, using operators like Where, Select, GroupBy, Join and OrderBy.|Over IQueryable it is translated to SQL; over IEnumerable it runs in memory.

IEnumerable: forward-only iteration.|ICollection: adds Count, Add, Remove and Contains.|IList: adds index access and Insert.|Accept the smallest interface you need; return read-only types such as IReadOnlyList.
First vs FirstOrDefault, Single vs SingleOrDefault?

First: the first match; throws if there is none. FirstOrDefault: returns default (null) instead.|Single: exactly one match; throws if none or more than one. SingleOrDefault: zero or one; throws if more than one.|Use Single for unique keys so duplicate data is caught.
Single = there can be only one.
Any() stops at the first match (EXISTS in SQL); Count() counts every row.|Use Any() to check existence; the Count property on a collection is already O(1).
Any = is anybody home? Count = take a census.

A lambda that captures variables from its outer scope; the compiler stores them in a hidden class so they live as long as the lambda.|Pitfalls: capturing a loop variable by mistake, or a large object that then cannot be collected.
The lambda packs a lunchbox from home.
Explain the Liskov Substitution Principle with an example.

Subtypes must work wherever the base type is expected, without changing correct behaviour.|Good: every ISftpClient provider honours the same contract, for example throwing SftpTransferException on failure and never failing silently.|Violation: a ReadOnlyRepository that throws NotSupportedException on Save; split the interface instead.
Swap the battery brand; the torch still works.
Explain Interface Segregation with an example.

Clients should not depend on methods they do not use.|Example: IShipmentReader for queries and IShipmentWriter for commands instead of one large IShipmentRepository, so a reporting service only gets read access and tests mock less.
Small menus, not one giant menu.
Explain Dependency Inversion with an example.

High-level modules depend on abstractions, not on concrete classes.|Example: VendorExchangeService depends on ISftpClient injected through ASP.NET Core DI; the Rebex implementation is registered in Program.cs, so business code never references Rebex.
Plug into the socket, not the power plant.
Why did you choose an interface?

To decouple callers from implementations (three SFTP libraries), enable DI and unit testing with Moq, and add providers without changing callers (open/closed).|A base class carries the shared code; the interface is the contract.
Interface = contract; base class = shared code.

When the relationship is not truly is-a, when behaviour varies independently (use strategy or composition), when hierarchies get deep, or across module boundaries where a base change breaks many children.
Has-a beats is-a when in doubt.
How does garbage collection affect performance?

Collections pause threads (briefly for Gen 0, longer for Gen 2), and high allocation rates trigger more collections, which raises p99 latency.|Reduce allocations: pooling (ArrayPool), Span<T>, no boxing, avoid large temporary strings and LOH objects; Server GC for throughput; measure with dotnet-counters.
What happens if an exception occurs inside an async method?

The exception is captured in the returned Task and rethrown at the await, with its stack trace.|If the Task is never awaited the exception is unobserved and lost; in `async void` it crashes the process.|With Task.WhenAll, await throws the first exception, and the task's Exception holds all of them.
The error waits inside the Task until you await it.
What is Dependency Injection and why do we use it?

A technique where an object receives its dependencies from outside, usually through its constructor, instead of creating them itself.|Why: loose coupling, testability (inject mocks), swapping implementations by configuration, and central lifetime management.
Don't build your tools; get them handed to you.
Any object a class needs to do its work, such as a repository, an HttpClient, a logger or an ISftpClient.
What is Inversion of Control, and what is an IoC container?

Inversion of Control: the framework, not your code, controls object creation and flow (don't call us, we'll call you); DI is one form of it.|An IoC container (the built-in ServiceCollection/ServiceProvider, Autofac) registers types, builds object graphs and manages lifetimes and disposal.
The container is the factory manager.

Constructor: dependencies are required, immutable and explicit; the default in ASP.NET Core.|Property: optional dependencies set after construction; the built-in container does not support it (Autofac does).|Too many constructor parameters means the class does too much.

The built container that resolves services (GetService), created from IServiceCollection when the host is built.|Scopes come from IServiceScopeFactory; HttpContext.RequestServices is the current request's scope.
Which lifetimes can depend on which (Singleton, Scoped, Transient)?

Rule: a service may depend on services that live at least as long as it does.|Singleton on Transient: allowed, but the transient effectively becomes a singleton. Singleton on Scoped: not allowed (captive dependency; scope validation throws in Development).|Scoped on Singleton or Transient: fine. Transient on Scoped: fine when resolved inside a scope.
Depend only on things that live at least as long as you.
GetService returns null if the service is not registered; GetRequiredService throws InvalidOperationException.|Prefer GetRequiredService to fail fast, and prefer constructor injection over both.
How does constructor injection work in ASP.NET Core, and how are controller dependencies resolved?

Controllers declare dependencies in their constructor. For each request the controller activator creates the controller from the request scope (HttpContext.RequestServices), resolving the whole graph recursively.|Minimal APIs inject handler parameters directly; [FromServices] works on action parameters.
Per request: new scope, new controller, wired graph.
How do you register and resolve multiple implementations of an interface?

Register several: `AddTransient<INotifier, EmailNotifier>()` and `AddTransient<INotifier, SmsNotifier>()`.|Inject `IEnumerable<INotifier>` to get all of them; a single INotifier gets the last registration.|.NET 8 keyed services: `AddKeyedScoped<ISftpClient, RebexClient>(key)` with `[FromKeyedServices(key)]`, or a factory that selects by configuration.
Many plugs: take the whole strip or ask by name.
Can you manually create a scope, and when would you use IServiceScopeFactory?

Yes: `using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();` then resolve from `scope.ServiceProvider`.|Use it in singletons and BackgroundServices that need scoped services such as DbContext, one scope per unit of work (for example per queue message).
Open a meeting room when you need one.
What is the service locator anti-pattern?

Pulling dependencies from IServiceProvider inside classes instead of declaring them in the constructor.|It hides dependencies, makes tests harder and fails at runtime; acceptable only in composition roots, factories and middleware.
How would you unit test a DI-based service?

Do not use the container: construct the class directly with Moq mocks for its interfaces, call the method, and assert outcomes and key interactions.|Test the wiring separately by building the ServiceProvider with ValidateOnBuild and ValidateScopes.
Unit tests use new, not the container.
Give a real DI example from your application.

VendorExchangeService receives ISftpClientFactory, IOptions<SftpOptions> and ILogger through its constructor; the factory returns the Rebex, SSH.NET or ComponentPro provider from configuration.|DbContext is Scoped, the RabbitMQ connection is a Singleton, validators are Transient.
Factory picks the plug; DI hands it over.
Why shouldn't everything be Singleton, or everything Transient?

Singleton: shared across threads and requests, so any state must be thread-safe, and holding scoped resources like DbContext causes captive-dependency bugs and stale data.|Transient everywhere: needless allocations, many instances of expensive objects, and no per-request sharing such as one unit of work.
Right lifetime for the right job.
What happens when a request ends?
The request's DI scope is disposed: every Scoped and Transient IDisposable created in it is disposed (DbContext closes its connection), and the HttpContext is returned for reuse.
Meeting over: lights off, room cleaned.
Who disposes Scoped and Singleton services, and how does DI handle IDisposable dependencies?

The container disposes what it created: scoped and transient disposables when their scope ends, singletons when the root provider is disposed at shutdown.|Instances you create yourself and register (`AddSingleton(new X())`) are not disposed by the container.|Avoid resolving transient disposables from the root provider: they live until shutdown, which is a leak.
Microsoft's cross-platform, open-source, high-performance framework for web APIs, MVC and real-time apps on modern .NET, with built-in DI, configuration, logging and the Kestrel server.
The cross-platform, async web server built into ASP.NET Core.|It runs on its own in containers or behind a reverse proxy or load balancer (ALB, IIS, Nginx) that handles TLS and extras.
Kestrel = the engine inside every ASP.NET Core app.
What happens if middleware is registered in the wrong order?

Things break quietly: UseAuthorization before UseAuthentication leaves the user anonymous (401/403); UseCors after the endpoints means no CORS headers; a late exception handler misses earlier errors; static files after auth forces auth on them.
Wrong order = guard checks tickets before checking ID.
Use: adds middleware that can call next.|Run: terminal middleware that ends the pipeline.|Map / MapWhen: branch the pipeline by path or condition.
Use = pass along, Run = stop here, Map = fork.

UseRouting matches the request to an endpoint early and stores it on HttpContext; middleware in between (CORS, auth) can read endpoint metadata such as [Authorize]; the endpoint runs at the end.|One routing system for controllers, minimal APIs, gRPC and health checks.
Pick the destination first, check the ticket, then travel.
Since .NET 6 the minimal hosting model merges Startup's ConfigureServices and Configure into Program.cs (`builder.Services...`, `app.Use...`). A Startup class still works if you keep one.

Not as server protection: CORS relaxes the browser's same-origin policy and does not stop curl, Postman or server-to-server calls.|Real security is authentication and authorization; CORS only controls which browser origins may read responses.
CORS is a browser courtesy, not a lock.

UseHttpsRedirection and UseHsts in production; certificates on Kestrel or, more commonly, TLS terminated at the ALB or API Gateway with ACM certificates, plus HTTPS between components where policy requires it.

AddHealthChecks with checks for the database, RabbitMQ and other dependencies, exposed with MapHealthChecks (for example /health/live and /health/ready).|Load balancers, ECS and Kubernetes use them to route traffic and replace unhealthy instances.
A pulse and a ready sign.
How do you implement graceful shutdown?

On SIGTERM the host stops accepting requests, lets in-flight ones finish within the shutdown timeout, and signals ApplicationStopping and the BackgroundService stopping token.|Consumers stop fetching, finish and ack current messages, then close connections; ECS and Kubernetes allow a grace period before killing the process.
Finish the plates on the table, take no new orders.
How do you handle cancellation tokens?

Accept a CancellationToken in actions (bound to HttpContext.RequestAborted) and pass it to EF Core, HttpClient and delays, so abandoned requests stop working.|Combine with timeouts via CancellationTokenSource.CancelAfter and handle OperationCanceledException quietly.
If the caller hangs up, stop cooking.
PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent; missing fields become defaults.|PATCH applies a partial change (JSON Patch or merge patch); use it to update a few fields.
PUT = replace the form; PATCH = correct one box.
200 OK: success with a body.|201 Created: a new resource was created; return a Location header and usually the resource.
400 Bad Request: invalid input.|401 Unauthorized: not authenticated (missing or invalid token).|403 Forbidden: authenticated but not allowed.
400 = bad form, 401 = who are you, 403 = not you.
404 Not Found: the resource or route does not exist.|405 Method Not Allowed: the route exists but not for this verb, for example DELETE on a read-only endpoint.
404 = wrong address; 405 = right address, wrong door.
409 Conflict: a valid request clashes with the current state (duplicate, concurrency version mismatch).|422 Unprocessable Entity: well-formed but semantically invalid (business validation fails).
409 = clash with reality; 422 = makes no sense.

500: unhandled error in this server.|502 Bad Gateway: a proxy or gateway got an invalid response from upstream.|503 Service Unavailable: overloaded or down (maintenance, no healthy targets); send Retry-After. 504 is an upstream timeout.
500 = I broke, 502 = my supplier broke, 503 = closed for now.
What are DTOs and why use them?

Data Transfer Objects: simple classes or records that shape exactly what an API accepts or returns.|Why: decouple the API contract from the DB schema, hide internal and sensitive fields, prevent over-posting, validate inputs and version independently.
DTO = the envelope, not the whole filing cabinet.
Why shouldn't you expose EF entities directly?

It leaks the schema and sensitive fields, couples clients to DB changes, enables over-posting, and causes serialization cycles and lazy-loading surprises.|Map to DTOs with Select projections, Mapster or AutoMapper.
Show the menu, not the kitchen.
DTO: the transport shape between layers or services (API contracts).|ViewModel: shaped for one UI view and may include display-only data. In APIs we mostly talk about DTOs.

An attribute that turns on API behaviours: attribute routing is required, invalid model state returns 400 ProblemDetails automatically, binding sources are inferred ([FromBody] for complex types), and errors use ProblemDetails.
What is routing, and attribute routing vs conventional routing?

Routing maps URLs to endpoints.|Attribute routing: `[Route(api/studies/{id})]` on controllers and actions; the standard for APIs.|Conventional routing: one template in Program.cs such as `{controller}/{action}/{id?}`; common for MVC sites.
Attribute = address on each door; conventional = one street map.
How do you implement filtering and sorting?

Query parameters such as `?status=Shipped&siteId=12&sortBy=shipDate&desc=true`.|Apply them to IQueryable before paging so SQL does the work; allow-list sortable and filterable fields to prevent injection and unindexed sorts; return the total count with the page.
Filter, sort, then page, all in SQL.
How do you document APIs, and what is Swagger/OpenAPI?

OpenAPI is the standard JSON/YAML description of an API; Swagger UI renders it interactively.|In .NET: Swashbuckle or the built-in Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi, XML comments, examples and auth settings; the contract is shared with consumers and used to generate clients.
How do you secure an API?

HTTPS only; authentication with JWTs from OIDC/SSO; authorization policies and resource-level checks; input validation; rate limiting; restricted CORS; security headers; no secrets or PHI in logs; dependency scanning; least-privilege DB and IAM roles; audit logging.
Lock, ID check, permission, limits, logs.

Access token: short-lived (for example [15 minutes]) and sent on every API call.|Refresh token: long-lived, stored securely and sent only to the identity provider to get new access tokens; it can be revoked server-side, which is how our logout fix works.
Access = day pass; refresh = membership card at reception.
Role-based vs policy-based authorization, and how do you implement policies?

Role-based: `[Authorize(Roles = StudyManager)]`; simple but coarse.|Policy-based: named policies with requirements and handlers registered in AddAuthorization, plus resource-based checks via IAuthorizationService (can this user access this study?).|Clinical systems need resource-level checks, not just roles.
Roles = job title; policies = specific rules.

Over-posting is when clients send extra fields that bind to properties they should not set (IsAdmin, Status).|Prevent it with input DTOs that contain only allowed fields; never bind entities directly.
Only accept what is on the form.
How do you handle large request payloads?

Limit size (MaxRequestBodySize, [RequestSizeLimit]), stream instead of buffering, compress, paginate responses, and send big files through presigned S3 uploads or chunked uploads instead of JSON bodies.
Big things go by freight, not in the envelope.
How do you handle file uploads?

IFormFile for small files, streaming (MultipartReader) for large ones; validate size, extension and content (magic bytes); scan for malware; store outside the web root (S3) with random names; process asynchronously.|Our CSV import used a [5 MB] limit, streamed parsing and validation before saving.
Check it, store it safely, process it later.
How do you design a production-ready API?

Contract: OpenAPI, versioning, DTOs, validation, ProblemDetails errors.|Security: authentication, authorization, rate limits, HTTPS.|Resilience: timeouts, retries, idempotency keys, health checks.|Observability: structured logs, correlation ids, metrics and alarms.|Performance: async, pagination, caching; tests and CI/CD with quality gates.

At every boundary, for its purpose: shape and format at the API (model validation or FluentValidation), business rules in the service/domain layer, and constraints in the database (keys, unique, check) as the last defence. UI validation is only for user experience.
Door, desk, and vault each check.
How do you prevent duplicate requests?

Idempotency key header: store the key with the result; on a repeat, return the stored result instead of executing again.|Back it with natural keys and unique constraints, optimistic concurrency, and disabling double-submit in the UI.
Same key, same answer, done once.

rows: Structured logs, correlation ids, metrics, alarms

QS: Microsoft's open-source ORM for .NET: it maps classes to tables, translates LINQ to SQL, tracks changes and manages migrations, with providers for SQL Server, PostgreSQL, SQLite and more.

ADO.NET: raw connections, commands and readers; fastest and most control, but manual SQL and mapping.|EF Core: LINQ, change tracking, migrations and productivity, with a small overhead.|Use EF Core for most CRUD, and Dapper or ADO.NET for hot paths and complex reporting SQL.
ADO.NET = manual gearbox; EF Core = automatic.
What is DbContext, and what is DbSet?

DbContext: a session with the database, combining unit of work, change tracker and connection management; the model is configured in OnModelCreating.|DbSet<T>: a queryable collection that represents a table, used to query, add and remove entities.
DbContext = the session; DbSet = a table inside it.

Include loads a navigation of the root entity; ThenInclude loads the next level from that navigation, for example `Studies.Include(s => s.Sites).ThenInclude(x => x.Shipments)`.|Deep includes can explode rows; consider AsSplitQuery or projections.
How do you create EF migrations?

`dotnet ef migrations add AddShipmentIndex` generates Up and Down code from model changes; review it like any code, then produce an idempotent script with `dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent` for the release.

Code First: the C# model is the source of truth and migrations create the schema.|Database First: scaffold entities from an existing database (`dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold`), good for legacy schemas owned by DBAs.
Code drives DB, or DB drives code.
LINQ queries over DbSet/IQueryable that EF Core translates into SQL and runs in the database; only translatable methods are allowed in the query.

Using methods EF cannot translate (custom C# functions, some string operations) inside a filter. EF Core 3+ throws instead of silently loading every row, except in the final Select projection.|Calling AsEnumerable or ToList too early also pulls data into memory before filtering.
If SQL can't say it, EF won't run it in the DB.
How do you optimize EF Core queries and performance?

AsNoTracking for reads; project to DTOs with Select; filter and page in SQL; avoid N+1 with Include or projections; AsSplitQuery for large includes.|Proper indexes, compiled queries for hot paths, ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete for bulk changes, DbContext pooling.|Log the generated SQL and check execution plans.
Track less, select less, round-trip less.
What is SaveChanges(), and SaveChanges() vs SaveChangesAsync()?
SaveChanges detects changes and writes every pending INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE in one transaction.|SaveChangesAsync does the same without blocking the thread during I/O; use it in ASP.NET Core.
One commit for all changes; async frees the thread.
How do you handle bulk operations?

EF Core 7+ ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete run set-based SQL without loading rows; AddRange with batching for inserts.|For very large loads use SqlBulkCopy or a bulk-extensions library, in chunks inside transactions.
Bulk = set-based, not row by row.
EF.CompileAsyncQuery caches the LINQ-to-SQL translation of a query shape, saving translation cost on very hot paths.|EF already caches most query plans, so use it only after measuring.
How do you log generated SQL?

`LogTo(Console.WriteLine)` on the options builder, or the Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command log category at Information; `ToQueryString()` on a query; EnableSensitiveDataLogging only in development.
See the SQL before you trust it.
How do you handle relationships: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many?

Configure with navigations and foreign keys by convention or Fluent API (HasOne/WithMany, HasMany/WithMany).|One-to-one: Subject and ConsentRecord. One-to-many: Site and Shipments. Many-to-many: Users and Studies, with an explicit join entity when the link has data (role, assigned date).
Properties that exist in the EF model and table but not in the C# class, such as LastModifiedBy or a foreign key, accessed with `EF.Property<T>(entity, name)`; handy for audit columns.
Value objects mapped as part of their owner with OwnsOne/OwnsMany, for example an Address inside Site stored in the Site table's columns; they have no identity of their own.
How do you configure indexes in EF Core?
Fluent API `HasIndex(s => new { s.StudyId, s.Status })` with IsUnique, HasFilter or IncludeProperties (SQL Server), or the [Index] attribute; created through migrations.
Index in code, built by migration.
What is a primary key, and what is a foreign key?

Primary key: uniquely identifies each row, not null, one per table (clustered by default in SQL Server).|Foreign key: a column referencing another table's primary key, enforcing referential integrity, with cascade rules.
PK = my ID; FK = my parent's ID.
What is a unique constraint, and primary key vs unique key?

A unique constraint forbids duplicate values and is backed by a unique index.|One primary key vs many unique keys; the PK is not null, while a unique key allows one NULL in SQL Server; the PK is the identity, unique keys are alternate keys such as KitNumber.
An index on several columns, such as (StudyId, Status, ShipmentDate). Column order matters: it supports seeks on the leading columns (leftmost prefix). Put equality columns first, then range columns.
Phone book: last name, then first name.
A non-clustered index with a WHERE clause (for example only Pending shipments): smaller and faster for queries on a hot subset. The query predicate must match the filter.
Index only the rows you search.
How do indexes improve performance, and when can they hurt?

Help: the B-tree lets SQL Server seek rows in logarithmic time instead of scanning, cover queries and avoid sorts.|Hurt: every insert, update and delete maintains them; they use storage and memory and cause page splits; unused or low-selectivity indexes are pure cost.

The optimizer's recipe for a query: operators (seeks, scans, join types, sorts), estimated vs actual rows and costs.|Read the actual plan (SSMS, Query Store) to find scans, key lookups, spills and bad estimates.
The plan is the query's GPS route.
Table scan vs index scan vs index seek?
Table scan: reads every row of a heap.|Index scan: reads all or a large range of an index.|Index seek: navigates the B-tree straight to the matching rows; best for selective predicates.
Scan = read the whole book; seek = open at the right page.
What is query cardinality, and what are statistics?

Cardinality estimate: how many rows the optimizer expects at each step of the plan.|Statistics: histograms of column value distribution used for those estimates. Stale statistics cause bad estimates and bad plans (our plan-regression incident).
Wrong guess of crowd size, wrong size of venue.
UNION removes duplicates, which costs a sort or hash; UNION ALL keeps every row and is faster. Use UNION ALL unless you need distinct rows.
EXISTS stops at the first match; IN compares against a list or subquery. Modern optimizers often produce the same plan.|NOT IN returns nothing if the subquery contains a NULL, so prefer NOT EXISTS.
NOT IN + NULL = surprise empty result.

CTE: a named query for one statement; not materialised; readable; supports recursion.|Temp table (#t): materialised in tempdb, can be indexed and reused across statements, and has statistics; better for large intermediate results.
CTE = sticky note; temp table = scratch notebook.
ROW_NUMBER: unique sequence even for ties.|RANK: ties share a rank and leave gaps.|DENSE_RANK: ties share a rank with no gaps.
Number, Rank with gaps, Dense without gaps.
How do you find duplicate records?
`SELECT KitNumber, COUNT(*) FROM Kits GROUP BY KitNumber HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;`|Or `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY KitNumber ORDER BY Id)` and keep row 1, which also lets you delete the extras.
How do you find the second-highest or nth-highest salary?

`SELECT DISTINCT Salary FROM Emp ORDER BY Salary DESC OFFSET N-1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY;`|Or `DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) = N`, which handles ties.|Second highest: `SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Emp WHERE Salary < (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Emp)`.
How do you get the top N records per group?
`WITH r AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY SiteId ORDER BY ShipDate DESC) AS rn FROM Shipments) SELECT * FROM r WHERE rn <= 3;`|Or CROSS APPLY with TOP N per group.
What are dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads?

Dirty read: reading uncommitted data that may be rolled back.|Non-repeatable read: the same row returns different values within one transaction because another transaction updated it.|Phantom read: re-running a range query returns new rows inserted by another transaction.
Dirty = unsaved, non-repeatable = changed, phantom = new.
Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: rules and constraints hold. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere. Durability: committed data survives crashes, thanks to the transaction log.

Optimistic: no locks; detect conflicts at write time with a rowversion; best for low contention (EF Core concurrency tokens).|Pessimistic: lock rows up front (UPDLOCK); for high-contention critical sections such as allocating the last drug kit.
Optimistic = check on save; pessimistic = lock before edit.
How do you optimize database performance?

Measure first (Query Store, wait stats, slow queries), then fix the top queries (indexes, SARGable predicates, rewrites).|Schema: right data types and normalisation; keep statistics and index maintenance current.|Scale reads with caching and read replicas; archive or partition old data; short transactions and connection pooling.
Measure, fix the worst, then scale.

Start from real query patterns. Clustered key: narrow, unique, ever-increasing.|Non-clustered on foreign keys and filter columns, equality columns first then range, INCLUDE the selected columns.|Check usage DMVs, remove unused and duplicate indexes, and weigh the write cost.
Index for the questions you actually ask.
An architecture of small, independently deployable services, each owning one business capability and its data, communicating over APIs or messages.
Small teams, small services, own data.
What are the advantages and disadvantages of microservices?

Advantages: independent deploys and scaling, fault isolation, team autonomy, technology choice per service.|Disadvantages: network latency and failures, distributed data and transactions, harder testing and debugging, more DevOps and observability work.
When would you NOT use microservices?

Small team or early product, unclear domain boundaries, low scale, no DevOps maturity (CI/CD, monitoring), or strong transactional consistency needed across the whole domain. Start with a modular monolith.
Don't build a fleet for one passenger.
How do you identify service boundaries, and what is a bounded context?

Use Domain-Driven Design: split by business capability and bounded context, the area where one model and its language stay consistent (Randomization, Supply, Shipments, Consent).|Signals: separate data ownership, different change rates and teams, few chatty calls between them.
One language per context, one service per context.
Synchronous REST or gRPC when the caller needs an immediate answer; asynchronous events or commands (Kafka, RabbitMQ) for decoupled workflows and notifications. Version every contract.
Ask with REST, announce with events.
REST vs messaging; synchronous vs asynchronous communication?

Synchronous (REST/gRPC): simple, immediate result, but temporal coupling; a slow callee slows the caller.|Asynchronous (queues/events): decoupled, absorbs spikes, resilient, but eventual consistency and harder tracing.
How services find each other's current addresses: DNS-based (Kubernetes Services, ECS Service Connect / Cloud Map) or load balancers, instead of hard-coded IPs as instances come and go.
A live phone book for services.

Retrying non-idempotent operations duplicates side effects; retrying permanent errors (400, 401, validation) wastes effort; aggressive retries amplify load into retry storms.|Retry only transient errors, with backoff, jitter and limits.
Retry the hiccup, not the refusal.
Separate resource pools per dependency (connection pools, concurrency limits, queues) so one slow dependency cannot exhaust every thread or connection, like watertight compartments in a ship.
One flooded room doesn't sink the ship.

Following one request across services with a trace id and spans (timing per hop), using OpenTelemetry and the W3C traceparent header; viewed in X-Ray, Jaeger or Grafana Tempo to find where latency or errors happen.

Data across services becomes consistent after a short delay rather than instantly; accepted for availability and decoupling. Design UIs and processes to tolerate it, for example with Pending statuses.
How do you handle failures between services?
Timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers and fallbacks; asynchronous messaging with durable queues and DLQs; idempotency; sagas with compensations; monitoring and alerts.

Version APIs (URL or header) and message contracts (additive changes, a schema version field); stay backward compatible; consumers tolerate unknown fields; deprecate with timelines; semantic-version the images.
Each service has its own pipeline: build, test, image, IaC. Deploy independently to ECS or Kubernetes with rolling or blue-green strategies, health checks and automated rollback.
Golden signals per service, centralised structured logs with correlation ids, distributed tracing, Grafana or CloudWatch dashboards, and alerts on SLOs, queue lag and DLQ depth.
How do you secure service-to-service communication?

Private networking (VPC, security groups) plus mTLS where required; service identities (OAuth client-credentials tokens or IAM roles); validate tokens and scopes on every call; least privilege; secrets in a vault. Never trust a caller just because of its network location.
Zero trust: every call shows ID.
How do you prevent cascading failures?
Timeouts everywhere, circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limiting and load shedding, async queues to absorb spikes, caching and graceful degradation; avoid long synchronous call chains.
Unit tests; integration tests with a real database and broker in containers; consumer-driven contract tests (Pact) between services; a few end-to-end tests; load and chaos tests for resilience.
Unit, integration, contract, a little E2E.
How do you manage configuration across services?
Environment variables plus central stores (AWS Parameter Store / Secrets Manager, Azure App Configuration), per-environment values managed by IaC, no secrets in images, and validation at startup.
One source of config truth per environment.
How do you handle centralized logging?
Structured JSON logs with correlation ids shipped to one place (CloudWatch Logs, OpenSearch, Loki), common fields (service, environment, version), retention policies, and no PHI or secrets.
All logs, one place, one format.
How would you design a scalable microservices architecture?

API gateway in front of stateless services on ECS or Kubernetes with autoscaling.|Database per service, Redis caching, read replicas.|Async events via Kafka/RabbitMQ with outbox and idempotent consumers.|Observability, CI/CD per service and resilience patterns throughout.
Gateway, stateless services, own data, events, eyes everywhere.
Why did you choose REST here?

For synchronous request/response needs: UI and partner calls that need an immediate answer (get a study, randomize a subject), where the client must know the result now. REST is simple, cacheable and widely understood.

When producers should not wait for or know their consumers, several consumers need the same events, replay and retention matter, and throughput is high, for example shipment status events used by several services.
What happens if Kafka is unavailable?

Producers buffer and retry (idempotent producer, delivery timeout) and then fail, so write events to an outbox table and publish later; consumers pause and resume from committed offsets; alert on broker health.|A multi-broker cluster with replication avoids a single point of failure.
Outbox keeps the letters until the post office reopens.
How do you guarantee exactly-once processing?

True end-to-end exactly-once across systems is rarely possible; achieve effectively-once with at-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers (dedupe by message id, upserts) and the outbox pattern.|Inside Kafka, idempotent producers and transactions give exactly-once read-process-write.

Requests come through API Gateway or an ALB to .NET Core services in Docker on ECS, in private subnets across two availability zones.|Data in RDS SQL Server (Multi-AZ) and DynamoDB, ElastiCache for caching, Lambda for event-driven pieces.|Logs and metrics in CloudWatch, dashboards in Grafana; infrastructure in CloudFormation and Terraform, deployed through Azure DevOps.
Gateway, containers, data, events, eyes, code-defined.

It was the company's chosen cloud for IRT. Its managed services (ECS, RDS, Lambda, DynamoDB) reduce operations work, it supports compliance for regulated workloads, and it has global regions and mature IaC tooling.

ECS: AWS-native, simpler, deep IAM and ALB integration, no control-plane fee.|EKS: managed Kubernetes, portable, huge ecosystem, but more complexity and cost.|Choose ECS for AWS-only simplicity, EKS to standardise on Kubernetes.
ECS = AWS's own; EKS = Kubernetes on AWS.
Serverless compute for containers on ECS or EKS: you set CPU and memory per task and AWS runs it, with no EC2 instances to patch or scale.
API Gateway vs Application Load Balancer?

API Gateway: API management features: auth (JWT, Lambda authorizers), throttling, usage plans, request validation, direct Lambda integration; priced per request.|ALB: layer 7 load balancing for HTTP to ECS/EC2 targets, path and host routing, cheaper at high steady volume, fewer API features.
Gateway = smart receptionist; ALB = traffic cop.
Serverless functions that run on events (API Gateway, S3, SQS, DynamoDB Streams, schedules); you pay per request and duration; scaling is automatic; maximum 15 minutes per run.
Code that wakes up on events.

The number of executions running at the same time. Accounts have a regional limit (1,000 by default); reserved concurrency caps or guarantees a function's share; provisioned concurrency keeps environments warm; excess requests are throttled.
How many copies run at once.

The maximum run time per invocation, configurable up to 15 minutes. Set it a little above the expected duration, align it with upstream timeouts (API Gateway has a 29-second default), and move longer work to Step Functions or ECS.
A fully managed NoSQL key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond latency at any scale, on-demand or provisioned capacity, streams, TTL and global tables.
What is a GSI, and what is an LSI?

GSI (global secondary index): a different partition and sort key, its own capacity, created any time, eventually consistent reads.|LSI (local secondary index): same partition key with a different sort key, must be created with the table, supports strongly consistent reads, 10 GB per partition-key limit.
Global = new drawer system; local = new order inside the same drawer.
What is RDS, and RDS vs an EC2-hosted database?

RDS: a managed relational database (SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL and others) with automated backups, patching, Multi-AZ failover and read replicas.|EC2-hosted: full control of the OS and settings, but you own patching, backups and high availability. Choose RDS unless you need that control.

Redis: in memory, sub-millisecond reads, rich data structures and TTL; ideal for caches, sessions, rate limits and locks, but not the system of record.|Database: durable, queryable, transactional source of truth.
Redis = desk drawer; database = filing archive.

Block Public Access, least-privilege bucket policies and IAM, encryption at rest (SSE-KMS) and in transit (HTTPS-only policy), versioning and Object Lock where needed, presigned URLs for temporary access, access logs and CloudTrail, VPC endpoints.
What is IAM, and IAM role vs user?

IAM controls who can do what on which AWS resources, through users, groups, roles and policies.|User: a long-term identity with credentials, for people (prefer SSO).|Role: an assumable identity with temporary credentials, for services (ECS task role, Lambda) and cross-account access; preferred.
User = permanent badge; role = visitor pass.
Logs: detailed event records, searchable with Logs Insights.|Metrics: numeric time series (CPU, latency, errors) for graphs and alarms; metric filters can turn log patterns into metrics.
Logs tell stories; metrics draw graphs.

Rules that watch a metric against a threshold over periods (for example 5xx over 1 percent for 5 minutes) and change state between OK and ALARM, triggering SNS notifications, autoscaling or other actions; composite alarms reduce noise.
A smoke detector on a metric.
How do you troubleshoot an AWS production issue?

Check scope and recent changes; CloudWatch dashboards and alarms (ALB 5xx, target health, ECS task restarts, RDS CPU and connections); Logs Insights by correlation id; ECS events (OOM kills, failed health checks); CloudTrail for config changes; AWS Health for service issues. Mitigate, then fix the cause.
How do you design disaster recovery?

Agree RTO and RPO with the business, then pick a strategy: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby or active-active.|Automated backups and cross-region copies, IaC to rebuild, replicated data (RDS cross-region replica, DynamoDB global tables, S3 replication), runbooks and regular DR drills.
RTO = how fast back; RPO = how much lost.

Automatically adjusting capacity to load: EC2 Auto Scaling groups, ECS service scaling, DynamoDB capacity. Target tracking (keep CPU near 60 percent), step or scheduled scaling; scale out fast, scale in slowly.
Security group: stateful, attached to instances or ENIs, allow rules only.|NACL: stateless, attached to subnets, allow and deny rules evaluated in order, return traffic must be allowed explicitly.
SG = door guard who remembers you; NACL = gate that checks both ways.

Lets resources in private subnets make outbound internet calls (package downloads, external APIs) without being reachable inbound; managed and per availability zone, charged per hour and per GB, so use VPC endpoints for AWS services.
How do containers access AWS services securely?

With an ECS task role (or Pod Identity / IRSA on EKS): the SDK credential chain gets temporary credentials automatically; no access keys in images or environment variables; least-privilege policies; VPC endpoints.

Secrets Manager: built for secrets, automatic rotation (RDS), cross-account sharing, priced per secret.|Parameter Store: config and secrets (SecureString), hierarchical, free standard tier, no built-in rotation.
Secrets Manager rotates; Parameter Store stores.
How do you reduce AWS cost?

Right-size tasks and instances, autoscaling and scale-to-zero for dev, Savings Plans or Reserved capacity, Spot for non-critical work, S3 lifecycle tiers, delete idle resources, VPC endpoints instead of NAT data, log retention policies, cost tags and budgets.
